The ironborn howled the Drowned God's name until the cliffs rang, and the child on the driftwood throne is a king twice over in their eyes tonight.

A duel is a duel; a war is a war. One champion's axe cannot sink my fleets, nor feed those starving rocks, nor conjure back the strength House Hoare spent holding the Trident all those years. The blockade holds, the sieges grind on, and a dragon need not be gallant twice.

#bold The Old Way won the beach. The new way will win the isles.#!

We met upon the strand before both hosts, in the old way, and the ironman's arm was every terrible thing his house's name promised. #bold The Old Way won the beach. The new way will win the isles.#!

fab_ac_iron_islands.0016.option1.text: A duel is not a war.

fab_ac_oldtown.0002.text: From the Mountains to the Sands

fab_ac_oldtown.0002.desc.text:
One realm remains south of everything I now hold: Dorne. And Dorne is like nothing I have yet faced.

The Martells of Sunspear have never been kings. Princes, they style themselves, in the fashion of the Rhoynar - the ten thousand ships of Nymeria made them what they are, and Nymeria's line has held Dorne against Storm King and Gardener alike for seven hundred years. Their deserts have swallowed every host that ever marched on them; their mountains have buried the rest. Their rule is Meria Martell, eighty years old, blind and immense - the Yellow Toad, her enemies call her, and her enemies have gained little by it. She wrote to me once already, offering alliance against Argilac as one equal to another. I refused her then. Now Argilac is dead, and there are no more equals.

So Rhaenys flies to Sunspear, to speak with the old princess beneath her own roof: the knee, or the dragon. Their words are #italic Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken#! - a proud boast for a people who have never yet met dragonfire.

#bold We shall see if they still lay claim to those words once they have faced the dragon.#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0003.desc.text:
Rhaenys' first raven from the south tells of a war unlike any we have fought.

A host of Dornish spearmen stood guard at the Prince's Pass, the gateway through the Red Mountains - so she did not go through the Red Mountains. Meraxes rose above the pass, above the red sands and the white, and came down upon the castle of Vaith to demand its submission.

She found it empty. Not taken, not fled in panic - emptied, deliberately, to the last spear and the last sack of grain. In the town beneath the walls only women and children and old men remained, drawing water and tending goats as though a dragon in the market square were no stranger than a dust storm. When my sister asked where their lords and fighting men had gone, they gave her one word, every one of them, courteous and closed as a shut gate:

#bold 'Away.'#!

Harren hid behind stone, and stone melted. Argilac came out to fight, and died. The Dornish mean to hide behind emptiness itself - and emptiness does not burn.

#bold Rhaenys flies on toward Sunspear. If the lords of Dorne will not receive her, their princess shall.#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0004.desc.text:
At Sunspear, the ancient seat of House Martell, my sister found the same defiant silence - the winding alleys of the shadow city deserted, the Old Palace unbarred and unguarded. But this castle was not quite empty. In her own hall, alone beneath the spear-and-sun banners, the Princess of Dorne sat waiting for the dragon.

Meria Martell has ruled Dorne for sixty years. She is eighty years of age, very fat, blind, and almost bald, her skin sallow and sagging - the Yellow Toad of Dorne, her enemies named her long ago, and most of those enemies are dust now while she still sits her chair. Neither age nor blindness has dulled her wits by so much as a hair, and she greeted the Queen of Westeros without rising, without fear, and without ceremony.

She offered no defiance of banners or hosts. She offered something harder to answer:

#bold 'I will not fight you, nor will I kneel to you. Dorne has no king. Tell your brother that.'#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0004.option1.text: #bold I shall - but we will come again, Princess... #!

fab_ac_oldtown.0004.option2.text: #bold ...and the next time, we shall come with fire and blood. #!

fab_ac_oldtown.0005.desc.text:
The old princess heard my sister's warning without so much as a flicker. Fire and blood, promised by a Targaryen queen with a dragon on her doorstep - and the Yellow Toad might have been listening to a fishwife complain about the weather. Then she gave her answer, and I suspect the singers will keep it longer than they keep most of what kings say:

#bold 'Your words. Ours are Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken. You may burn us, my lady ... but you will not bend us, break us, or make us bow. This is Dorne. You are not wanted here. Return at your peril.'#!

Thus queen and princess parted, and Dorne remained unconquered.

An old blind woman alone in an empty castle has done what Harren's stone and Argilac's storm and the iron fist of the Two Kings could not: she has sent a Targaryen home without a submission. I will not pretend the audacity of it does not command a certain respect - nor that it changes anything. Dorne's reckoning is deferred, not forgiven.

#bold The toad keeps her deserts - for now. There is a crown waiting for me in Oldtown first.#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0005.option1.text: Queen and princess parted, with Dorne still beyond the Iron Throne.

fab_ac_oldtown.0006.desc.text:
They tell me the dragon queen found Vaith just as I arranged it: the castle bare, the granaries carted away, and no soul left in the town but grandmothers and babes with one word to give her. Away. You cannot burn away.

And so she came to Sunspear, as I knew she must, and found me waiting alone in my own hall. I am eighty years old, blind, fat and nearly bald — my enemies named me the Yellow Toad half a century ago, and I have buried nearly all of them since. A dragon on my doorstep does not hurry my pulse.

I told her plainly: I will not fight you, nor will I kneel to you. Dorne has no king. Tell your brother that.

She promised to come again with fire and blood. Their little words. I gave her ours — unbowed, unbent, unbroken — and sent her home to her brother with nothing. The kings of grass and river may kneel. This is Dorne.

fab_ac_oldtown.0006.option1.text: Queen and princess parted, and Dorne still bowed to no one.

fab_ac_oldtown.0007.desc.text:
The dragon queen crossed the Red Mountains the only way that costs Dorne nothing — over them — and found Vaith emptied to the last spear, exactly as my mother planned it before the gods took her. The Yellow Toad is gone, but her design outlives her, and I have not moved a stone of it.

So Rhaenys Targaryen came at last to Sunspear, and found not the old woman she had prepared her courtesies for, but me, alone in the hall my mother sat for sixty years.

I gave her the answer I inherited along with the chair. I will not fight her; there is nothing here for her dragon to fight. I will not kneel to her; Dorne has no king to be conquered. She promised fire and blood, as her house does. I gave her our words back — unbowed, unbent, unbroken — and let the empty sands say the rest.

fab_ac_oldtown.0007.option1.text: Queen and prince parted, and Dorne still bowed to no one.

fab_ac_oldtown.0008.desc.text:
The dragon queen crossed the Red Mountains the only way that costs Dorne nothing — over them — and found Vaith emptied to the last spear, exactly as my mother planned it before the gods took her. The Yellow Toad is gone, but her design outlives her, and I have not moved a stone of it.

So Rhaenys Targaryen came at last to Sunspear, and found not the old woman she had prepared her courtesies for, but me, alone in the hall my mother sat for sixty years.

I gave her the answer I inherited along with the chair. I will not fight her; there is nothing here for her dragon to fight. I will not kneel to her; Dorne has no king to be conquered. She promised fire and blood, as her house does. I gave her our words back — unbowed, unbent, unbroken — and let the empty sands say the rest.

fab_ac_oldtown.0008.option1.text: Queen and prince parted, and Dorne still bowed to no one.

fab_ac_oldtown.0009.desc.text:
Meraxes has come home, and my sister with her - empty-handed for the first time in this conquest. She is not accustomed to it. Neither am I.

We have talked long into the night of what a Dornish war would mean, and the truth sits ill with both of us. There is no host to break there, no proud king to meet me in the field, no castle whose burning would end it - only sand, thirst, empty keeps, and spears that strike from the rocks and are gone. Dragons win battles; Dorne offers none. To conquer the deserts would cost me years and legions, and the realm I have just stitched together is too new for either.

So Dorne keeps its sands, and the old woman keeps her chair - for now. No one should mistake patience for pardon.

#bold South and west, then, to the one great gate that has yet to open: Oldtown, the High Septon, and the Hightower. It is time the Faith met the dragon.#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0010.desc.text:
The Hightower rises above the horizon long before Oldtown's walls come into view, its beacon a pale flame against the southern sky. Beneath it lies the greatest city in Westeros: the Citadel and its grey scholars, the Starry Sept and the Father of the Faithful, wharves crowded with half the wealth of the realm, and more souls than some kingdoms can boast.

The High Septon has spent seven days and seven nights in prayer. Word carried from the city says the Crone showed him Oldtown consumed by dragonfire should the Hightowers resist me. Yet visions do not open gates, and holy counsel does not always master a proud lord.

My host advances along the roseroad beneath the three-headed dragon. Soon the walls sharpen through the morning haze, and the beacon atop the Hightower changes before my eyes.

#bold Now shall I learn whether Oldtown has heeded the Crone's lamp. #!

fab_ac_oldtown.0010.a.text: The dragon flies above open gates. Oldtown has chosen wisely.

fab_ac_oldtown.0010.b.text: The beacon burns green. Oldtown has called its banners.

fab_ac_oldtown.0011.desc.text:
Green fire blazes from the crown of the Hightower.

The gates are barred. A great chain closes the Honeywine, and every bell in Oldtown calls men not to prayer, but to arms. From the orchards and villages beyond the walls come the banners of House Hightower's sworn swords, answering the green flame above their city. The High Septon counselled submission; pride has answered in his stead.

My captains warn that even a short siege will cost gold, men, and time. Oldtown's walls are strong, but stone has failed before me from Harrenhal to the Eyrie, and no wall can close the sky.

#bold The Crone showed them fire. Lord Hightower has chosen to look upon it with his own eyes. #!

fab_ac_oldtown.0011.a.text: Close every road and raise the dragons. Oldtown will open its gates.

fab_ac_oldtown.0012.desc.text:
It is finished. The banners of the Honeywine are scattered, the harbour is his, and the three-headed dragon flies from the Hightower where the beacon-flame burns. His beasts circle the tower as I write — slowly, without haste, the way a victor circles.

We wagered ten thousand years of the Hightower's keeping against an old man's vision of fire, and the vision has collected its debt. My sword is surrendered, my knee is bent. That the city was not burned outright is a mercy I did not earn.

His High Holiness — who counselled submission from the first — is to crown the conqueror in the Starry Sept in three days' time. The gods forgive us. The Crone did try to light the way.

fab_ac_oldtown.0013.desc.text:
The seven oils are still wet upon my brow when I rise.

Above me there is no crystal dome to catch the morning light. Shards of it lie melted among the blackened stones, and the faces of the Seven stare down from cracked alcoves through veils of smoke. The High Septon found the holy oils beneath a fallen altar. He anointed me where the Starry Sept once stood whole, his hands steady though ash clung to his robes.

Beyond the ruin, Oldtown is silent. No fathers lift their children to see Balerion. No cheering follows my crown through the streets. The Hightower's beacon burns red once more, but beneath it the three-headed dragon flies above broken gates.

I have the blessing of the Faith and the submission of the city, as I came to claim. Yet the oldest sept in Westeros is a smoking shell, the Honeywine is choked with wreckage, and every godly lord in my new-made realm will remember the price of this anointing.

#bold A realm may be hammered into one upon an anvil of stone. It does not follow that the stone will forgive the hammer. #!

fab_ac_oldtown.0013.a.text: The ashes bear witness. I am anointed king.

fab_ac_oldtown.0015.desc.text:
The greatest city in Westeros did not make me break a single lance for it. As my host came within sight of the Hightower's flame, we found the gates of Oldtown standing open - and Lord Manfred Hightower waiting on the road to offer me his sword, his city, and his oath.

The why of it is a stranger tale than the walls themselves. When word of my landing first reached Oldtown, the High Septon shut himself within the Starry Sept for seven days and seven nights, fasting on bread and water, praying at one altar after the next. On the seventh day, he emerged to declare that the Crone had raised her golden lamp and shown him the path ahead: if Oldtown took up arms against the dragon, Oldtown would burn - the Hightower, the Citadel, and the Starry Sept cast down and destroyed. Lord Manfred is a cautious and a godly man - one son sworn to the Warrior's Sons, another lately a septon - and he heard his Father of the Faithful. Not one man of Oldtown burned on the Field of Fire, though the Hightowers were sworn to Highgarden of old.

So the lord knelt on the road before me and Balerion both, and made his offers - and one offer more: the hand of his youngest daughter. I declined her with every courtesy. A man with two queens does well not to collect a third.

#bold And within the city, they say, His High Holiness is waiting for me. The gods of the Seven wish to crown what the sword has already won.#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0015.option1.text: The Crone lit her lamp in good time, my lord. Rise.

fab_ac_oldtown.0016.text: The Coronation of Aegon I Targaryen

fab_ac_oldtown.0016.desc.text:
Three days after the gates of Oldtown opened to me, I knelt beneath the dome of the Starry Sept - the black marble heart of the Faith itself - and His High Holiness anointed my brow with the seven oils, set a crown upon my head, and proclaimed me before gods and men:

#bold Aegon of House Targaryen, the First of His Name, King of the Andals, the Rhoynar, and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms, and Protector of the Realm.#!

Seven Kingdoms, His High Holiness said - though Dorne remains unbowed. The style can stand as a promise.

A bare handful of lords stood witness when Visenya first crowned me at the Aegonfort; hundreds filled the Starry Sept today, and among them the maesters and archmaesters of the Citadel in their rings and masks and robes. The grey scribes record what the grey scribes witness - I do not doubt that when the histories are written, it is this day, and not the crowning by the Blackwater, that they will fix as the first of my reign. So be it. A king can be crowned twice; a realm is only forged once.

#bold Thus are the Seven Kingdoms of Westeros hammered into one realm - by my will, my sisters' fire, and now the blessing of the gods the most of my subjects hold most dear.#!

fab_ac_oldtown.0016.option1.text: Seven oils, one realm, one king.

fab_ac_oldtown.0016.option2.text: I accept the crown - but the gods of Valyria keep my house.

fab_ac_coronation.0001.desc.text:
The Starry Sept gave me a crown; the streets of Oldtown gave me something rarer.

When the rites were done, I did not return to my host in a litter or beneath a canopy, as the septons no doubt expected of an anointed king. I mounted Balerion in the sept's own square and rode him through the city at a walk - down the winding cobbled streets, past the guildhalls and the wharves, beneath the shadow of the Hightower itself, his wings folded and his black scales shining, my crown still on my brow.

Tens of thousands came out to see it. They packed the streets and the rooftops and hung from the windows, fathers lifting children onto their shoulders to look upon the Black Dread - the greatest beast in the world, walking their streets tame as a palfrey with their new king upon his back. There were screams at first. Then cheering, wave upon wave of it, rolling ahead of us from street to street until the whole city roared.

Fear brought Westeros to its knees. But fear rusts, and crowns won by fear alone rust with it. What Oldtown saw today it will tell for three generations: not the dragon that burns, but the dragon that need not.

#bold Every kingdom will hear how Oldtown cheered. The conquest ends not when they kneel - but when they cheer.#!

fab_ac_coronation.0001.option1.text: Remember this day. So shall I.

fab_ac_coronation.0002.desc.text:
The war is over. Six kingdoms bow to one crown, and now every lord and merchant and septon in Westeros asks the same question of me: where shall that crown live?

Dragonstone is the seat of my fathers - a fortress no fleet has ever taken, raised by Valyrian hands in the old way, with the salt and the smoke in its very stones. It is strong, it is mine, and it is where my line began. But it stands on an island at the edge of my realm, and a king who rules from the edge of his realm will find that the middle forgets him.

Then there is the hill where I first came ashore, at the mouth of the Blackwater. The Aegonfort is timber and mud, and the town rising around it is younger than my reign - but it stands where the realm's roads and rivers meet. The smallfolk have already given the place a name. They call it King's Landing.

My court must sit somewhere. It is for me to choose.

fab_ac_coronation.0002.option1.text: My throne shall stand at King's Landing.

fab_ac_coronation.0002.option2.text: Dragonstone shall remain the seat of my rule.

fab_ac_coronation.0002.option4.text: Harren built his towers to last forever. Now they serve a dragon.

fab_ac_coronation.0002.option5.text: My court shall sit at Oldtown, the oldest and greatest of cities.

fab_ac_coronation.0003.text: The Forging of the Iron Throne

fab_ac_coronation.0003.desc.text:
The Seven Kingdoms are mine, and a conqueror must have a seat worthy of them. I have given a command: that every blade raised against me - the swords of fallen kings and broken lords, gathered from the Blackwater to the Trident and the very gates of Storm's End - be carried here and laid before me.

We heap them high beneath the open sky, and I bid Balerion breathe. The Black Dread's fire runs white-hot, hot enough to melt a thousand blades into one. For days the smiths labour, beating the twisted, half-melted steel into a single monstrous chair - jagged, barbed and cruel, sharp enough to bite a careless hand.

The realm is already calling it the #bold Iron Throne#!. It is no comfortable seat, and I would not have it so. A king should never sit easy.

fab_ac_coronation.0003.option1.text: A king should never sit easy.

fab_ac_coronation.0004.desc.text:
The hall is full today, and the world outside it has changed.

My sisters stand at my sides, as they have stood since Dragonstone - Visenya at my right hand, Dark Sister at her hip even here; Rhaenys at my left, whose smile no man in this hall begrudges her. Below the throne the great lords of Westeros stretch back to the doors, and where once each of them looked to a different crown, now every eye in the realm turns to a single seat of fused and blackened steel.

I think of it as a single land now, and it is a strange thing to hold in the mind. From the Wall in its cold to the red mountains of the south, one law, one peace, one king. The rivers that men bled over for a thousand years run through one realm. The roads run unbroken. A merchant may ride from White Harbor to the Arbor and never cross a border under arms. What a hundred kings could not do in a hundred lifetimes, three dragons have done in a handful of years.

The maesters may keep their ledgers of which kingdom bent first and which was hardest to bring low. Those are small accountings, and they will be forgotten. This is what will be remembered: that the sky over Westeros belongs to House Targaryen, and shall belong to us for a thousand years and a thousand more. Long after my bones are dust and my sisters' names are songs, men will look up and know whose blood rules them. They will call us the House of the Dragon, and they will be right to.

And yet the land is not wholly one. South of the marches the sands lie quiet, and an old blind woman sits in Sunspear who told my sister that Dorne has no king to bend the knee, and sent my threats back to me unopened. Hers is the one banner in all of Westeros that has never dipped before my dragons.

#bold The realm is very nearly whole. Only Dorne stands apart - and whether it stands so for a season or for all time is mine to decide.#!

fab_ac_coronation.0004.option1.text: We did warn Princess Meria that we would return with Fire and Blood.

fab_ac_coronation.0004.option2.text: Dorne shall remain Unbowed, Unbent, Unbroken.

fab_ac_coronation.0005.desc.text:
The conquest is done, and the realm must now be taught to live with it.

From the Wall to the Dornish marches, the banners of the conquered kings are struck or sworn. Save only for the sun-scorched lords of Dorne, who keep to their sands and their spite, every great house of Westeros now bends to [ROOT.Char.GetFirstName].

No longer is [ROOT.Char.GetFirstName] merely the Lord of Dragonstone, nor a conqueror with a half-forged crown. From this day [ROOT.Char.GetFirstName] is #bold King of the Andals, the Rhoynar and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms and Protector of the Realm#!.

And with the realm made one, one law above all others is proclaimed to every corner of it: the #bold King's Peace#!. From this day, no lord great or small - whatever his rank, whatever his grievance - shall make war upon his neighbor or settle his disputes with fire and steel. The private wars that bled Westeros for a thousand years are ended; justice belongs to the king's law, the king's courts, and the king's peace. Those who break it will answer to the Iron Throne - and the Iron Throne has dragons.

The lords will feast and swear their oaths anew. The dragon has brought peace to a land that knew only war - and, for now, the realm is one.

fab_ac_coronation.0005.option1.text: The Seven Kingdoms are almost one.

fab_bm_conquest_desc.text:
2 BC. Westeros is seven quarrelsome kingdoms, ruled by seven proud crowns that have warred upon one another since the Andals came. On a smoking island off the eastern shore, a young lord studies a painted table carved in the shape of the whole continent - and looks west.

Aegon Targaryen holds no great host, no deep treasury, no ancient claim. He holds Dragonstone, two sister-queens, and three dragons - the last dragons in all the world, and the only argument he will ever need. Balerion the Black Dread, Vhagar and Meraxes against the assembled might of Westeros: the harpers will call it madness right up until the moment they call it destiny.

#bold Seven kingdoms. One dragon's dream. Fire and blood. #!

bookmark_fab_aegon_desc.text:
[Concept( 'story_content_fab_aegon', '$bm_story_content_available_icon|q$' )|E] [Concept( 'story_content_fab_aegon', '$bm_story_content_available_copy|q$' )|E]
The Lord of Dragonstone is a riddle even to those who love him: solitary, brooding, a man who takes counsel from no one save his two sister-wives - and dreams, some whisper, of things not yet come to pass. Now the riddle has an answer, and the answer is conquest. Astride Balerion the Black Dread, with Visenya and Rhaenys at his wings, Aegon means to make seven kingdoms into one.

#bold The Conqueror's war begins. Will history remember the man who forged Westeros - or the fool who burned upon its spears? #!

bookmark_fab_harren_desc.text: Forty years House Hoare has bled the riverlands to raise Harrenhal, the greatest castle the world has ever seen - and now, at last, its towers stand finished. Harren the Black is old, cruel, and utterly certain: no army can breach those walls, and no king alive commands the strength to try.\n\n#bold But the doom of Harrenhal comes on wings. Can the ironborn king defy the fire that history has written for him? #!

bookmark_fab_harren_subheading.text: King of the Isles and the Rivers

bookmark_fab_torrhen_desc.text: The North remembers a thousand years of Stark kings, and Torrhen means to keep faith with every one of them. When the dragons come, he will call his banners and march his thirty thousand south - to a riverbank where he must weigh the oldest crown in Westeros against the lives of every man behind him.\n\n#bold History names him the King Who Knelt. But history has not yet been written - will you kneel, or will the North burn rather than bow? #!

bookmark_fab_meria_desc.text: Blind, gouty, near eighty, and more dangerous than any knight in her sandy dominion: Meria Martell, the Yellow Toad of Dorne, has outlived every rival who ever laughed at her. She will not meet the dragons in the field - the sands themselves will fight for her, and Dorne cannot be conquered by anyone who cannot find it.\n\n#bold 'You may burn us, my lady - but you will not bend us, break us, or make us bow.' Prove it. #!

bookmark_fab_loren_desc.text: The gold of Casterly Rock has made Loren Lannister the richest king in Westeros, but no treasure can buy safety from dragonfire. With the Westerlands behind him and the Reach beside him, the Last King of the Rock commands a host vast enough to bury lesser conquerors beneath its banners.\n\n#bold Can Loren turn the Field of Fire into the grave of Aegon's ambitions and keep the Rock beneath a Lannister crown? #!

bookmark_fab_mern_desc.text: House Gardener has ruled from Highgarden since the dawn of legend, and Mern IX will not be the king who lets that ancient line wither. The Reach can field more swords than any realm in Westeros, while alliance with Loren Lannister places an army of overwhelming strength at Mern's side. Yet even the greatest harvest may be consumed by fire.\n\n#bold Can the last Gardener king break the dragons and preserve the green crown of the Reach? #!

bookmark_fab_argilac_desc.text:
[Concept( 'story_content_fab_argilac', '$bm_story_content_available_icon|q$' )|E] [Concept( 'story_content_fab_argilac', '$bm_story_content_available_copy|q$' )|E]
Argilac the Arrogant is old, but the warrior who shattered a Dornish invasion has lost none of his fury. His offer of land and marriage was answered by Aegon Targaryen with a bastard's hand for his only daughter—an insult no Storm King could endure. Now the gathering storm will break upon dragons.

#bold Will Argilac cast the invaders back into the narrow sea, or will House Durrandon die with its last king? #!

bookmark_fab_ronnel_desc.text: Ronnel Arryn wears an ancient crown while still a child, leaving the rule of Mountain and Vale in the capable hands of his mother, Sharra. The Bloody Gate and the Eyrie's heights have humbled every earthbound invader—but Aegon's queens do not need roads, and their dragons can soar above the strongest walls.\n\n#bold Can the boy king and his regent keep the Vale beyond the conqueror's reach? #!

game_concept_story_content_fab_aegon_des.text: #tooltip_heading Story Style: Extensive#!\n\nAs Aegon Targaryen, you will take Westeros one kingdom at a time. Scripted events carry the war from the landing at the Blackwater to Harrenhal, the Field of Fire, the king who kneels in the North and the long grinding war in Dorne, and follow the crown you build once the fighting stops.

game_concept_story_content_fab_argilac_d.text: #tooltip_heading Story Style: Moderate#!\n\nAs Argilac Durrandon, you will answer for the envoy you sent back without his hands. Scripted events follow the Storm King's war against Aegon and Orys Baratheon, the stormlords you call to arms, and what becomes of your daughter and your crown when the dragons come.

fab_dorne_first_war_decision.text: Bring Dorne Beneath the Iron Throne

fab_dorne_first_war_decision_desc.text: Six kingdoms kneel; the seventh hides behind its sands. The Yellow Toad told my sister that Dorne has no king to conquer — and promised us peril if we returned.\n\nWe warned her what our answer would be. Fire and Blood.

fab_dorne_first_war_decision_desc_deferr.text: I named the first war finished before the council, but I never named it settled. Orys still sits in a Dornish cell, Highgarden's lord still lies unfound in the sands, and the old woman still calls herself unbowed.\n\nThe deserts have had their rest. Fire and blood, until Dorne remembers.

fab_dorne_first_war_decision_tooltip.text: The Conquest is unfinished while Dorne stands apart.

fab_crown_vale_war_decision_desc.text: The Falcon still perches above the clouds and calls itself a king. Mountains and waycastles turned back our first attempt — but no pass is high enough to shut out a dragon.\n\nThe Vale will be brought into the realm. Fire and Blood.

fab_crown_vale_war_decision_tooltip.text: The Conquest is unfinished while the Vale stands apart.

fab_crown_north_war_decision_desc.text: The Kings of Winter still rule beyond the Neck as they have for eight thousand years, and our first crossing was thrown back at the causeway.\n\nThe realm cannot be whole while half its lands owe it nothing. The North will kneel. Fire and Blood.

fab_crown_north_war_decision_tooltip.text: The Conquest is unfinished while the North stands apart.

fab_ac_defender.0001.desc.text: A Lyseni trader is ushered into my war council beneath a cloud of perfume, sea-salt, and expensive confidence. His wagons, he claims, carry engines built around immense torsion arms: scorpions capable of hurling iron bolts high enough to threaten even a dragon in flight.\n\nThe merchant makes no promise that his engines will slay Balerion. He merely smiles and observes that even the Black Dread must descend before dragonfire can reach my ranks. For half the usual price of a siege regiment, his artificers and their weapons will be mine before the next battle.

fab_ac_defender.0001.a.text: Buy the scorpions. Dragons bleed too.

fab_ac_defender.0001.a.tt.text: One [GetMaA('scorpions').GetName] regiment joins your forces for half the recruitment cost of a mangonel regiment.

fab_ac_defender.0001.b.text: Send the Lyseni and his machines away.

fab_ac_defender.0100.desc.text:
Aegon Targaryen has sent his demand to Storm's End. I am to lay down the crown of Durran Godsgrief, bend my knee, and hold the stormlands by his leave. In return, the heathen promises that my house, my lands, and my lords will be spared. If I refuse, his armies will come south and his dragon with them.

He speaks as though the matter were already settled. Perhaps every lord who has knelt before him has taught him to expect obedience. He will find no such lesson here. My fathers held these lands against ironborn, Dornishmen, Andals, and every other enemy the gods saw fit to send against them. Storm's End has stood through a thousand years of war, and I did not wear Durran's crown this long to surrender it because a Valyrian boy arrived with a beast and called himself king.

Yet it is not only my crown that will burn if I choose wrongly. Every man who rides beneath the crowned stag has a wife, a son, a hall, or a field behind him. The Seven know I have never been called craven, but there are deaths a king may command for honor and deaths he commands only for pride.

Aegon will have his answer.

#bold If I bend, men may call me craven. If I do not, no man will ever dare it.#!

fab_ac_defender.0100.a.text: I will not burn the stormlands for my pride. I yield the crown.

fab_ac_defender.0100.b.text: Sound the muster. The heathen will learn what king he has challenged.

fab_ac_defender.0110.desc.text: Aegon Targaryen offers the Reach the peace of submission. If I bend the knee, our fields and castles will be spared the dragon's flame. If I refuse, the green hand will close around its sword and the war will continue to its true conclusion.

fab_ac_defender.0120.desc.text: The dragonlord demands the Rock's allegiance and the crown of the Westerlands. Submission would preserve my house beneath his new order; refusal means trusting gold, stone, and western steel against dragonfire. Aegon's victories do not make this choice for me.

fab_ac_defender.0130.desc.text: Aegon Targaryen demands that Dorne bow with the other kingdoms. He promises peace beneath his rule and fire for every holdfast that resists. Yet deserts have swallowed greater hosts than his, and a dragon cannot burn what it cannot find. I must answer.

fab_ac_defender.0140.desc.text: Aegon Targaryen demands the submission of Harren's dominion and the crown of the Iron Isles. To kneel may preserve what remains; to refuse is to trust black walls, ironborn resolve, and the waters of the Trident against the Black Dread.

fab_ac_defender.0150.desc.text: Aegon Targaryen has come ashore to make the Crownlands the foundation of his new realm. His terms are simple: swear fealty and be spared, or hold fast and decide the matter by war. Dragonfire is terrible, but surrender is no longer inevitable.

fab_ac_defender.0160.desc.text: The Two Kings rode together so neither the Reach nor the Rock would face Aegon's dragons alone. Now the conqueror demands my submission. If the western king is governed by his own counsel, I cannot kneel on his behalf; I can only hold to our pact and fight.

fab_ac_defender.0170.desc.text: The Two Kings rode together so neither the Rock nor the Reach would face Aegon's dragons alone. Now the conqueror demands my submission. If the Reach's king is governed by his own counsel, I cannot kneel on his behalf; I can only hold to our pact and fight.

fab_ac_defender.0180.desc.text: Aegon's host has crossed into the North, and his demand follows it: lay down the ancient crown and preserve my people beneath his new throne, or trust the neck, the cold, and northern steel against dragonfire. This choice will be mine, not the dragon's.

fab_ac_defender.0190.desc.text: The dragon has come for the Vale. Aegon offers peace beneath his crown if I yield the Falcon Crown; refusal means testing mountain, knight, and scorpion against creatures that own the sky. The war will not decide itself before I answer.

fab_ac_defender.0200.desc.text: Again the dragonlord demands that Dorne abandon its defiance. He offers an end to war beneath his Iron Throne, while every pass and desert road still invites resistance. I may spare Dorne another campaign—or make Aegon win every league of it.

fab_ac_defender.1000.desc.text: The war for the Crownlands is over. Aegon Targaryen's banners stand above the roads and rivers I could not hold, and the Black Dread circles a realm that must now answer to the dragonlord. Whether by defeat or by my own submission, the issue has been settled, and my banners must come down.

fab_ac_defender.1010.desc.text: The war for the Kingdom of the Isles and the Rivers is finished. The Trident answers to the dragon now, the longships have been dragged home, and the crown Harwyn Hoare took by force has been taken back the same way.\n\nHarrenhal was raised so that no army of men could ever bring this house down. Against men the walls were answer enough. They were never an answer for this.

fab_ac_defender.1010.desc.harren.text:
Forty years I spent on these stones. Forty years of ironborn sweat and riverland gold, and every mason who thought the work too slow was set to some slower work still. When the last tower went up I was the mightiest lord in Westeros, and I had the walls to prove it.

The dragonlord never threw them down. He did not need to. He took the rivers, and the isles, and the men who were meant to hold them, and left me the castle.

Harrenhal stands. My kingdom does not.

fab_ac_defender.1010.desc.submit.text:
I have yielded, and there will be songs about it, and not one of them kind.

Forty years I spent raising Harrenhal so that no army raised by man could ever take it from me. The dragonlord did not bring an army of men. He offered me my life and the isles my fathers held, and asked only for the crown — and a crown is a smaller thing than a man's own bones burned black in his own hall.

The Kingdom of the Isles and the Rivers is ended. I am not.

fab_ac_defender.1010.a.text: The kingdom is lost. The walls are not.

fab_ac_defender.1010.a.submit.text: They can sing what they like. The isles endure.

fab_ac_defender.1020.desc.text: The fate of the Stormlands is decided at last. Whether by defeat in the field or by my own decision to spare the realm further fire, Storm's End now stands beneath Aegon Targaryen's new crown. The storm has spent itself before the dragon.

fab_ac_defender.1030.desc.text: The captains and kings of the Iron Isles resisted until the war was lost. Aegon Targaryen has taken the crown, and the dragon's terms can no longer be refused. The isles must reckon with a new order beyond their grey shores.

fab_ac_defender.1030.desc.submit.text: I have chosen to yield the Iron Islands before dragonfire exacts a price no crown can repay. Aegon Targaryen takes the crown and my oath, but the captains, keeps, and people of the isles survive to reckon with the new order beyond their grey shores.

fab_ac_defender.1030.a.text: The iron price was not enough.

fab_ac_defender.1100.desc.text: Ravens bring word that [fab_ac_news_a.GetShortUINamePossessive] realm has fallen to Aegon Targaryen. The war could no longer be sustained, and another crown now lies beneath the shadow of the Black Dread. Across Westeros, every court measures the distance between its own walls and the conqueror's host.

fab_ac_defender.1110.desc.text: The ravens carry tidings from the west: both the Reach and the Westerlands now answer to Aegon Targaryen. Two ancient crowns have fallen beneath the dragon, and the conqueror turns his gaze toward the kingdoms that remain beyond his grasp.

fab_ac_defender.1110.a.text: Two more crowns beneath the dragon.

fab_ac_defender.1120.desc.text: Against all expectation, Aegon Targaryen has forced Dorne to yield. [fab_ac_news_a.GetShortUINamePossessive] resistance is ended, and the southernmost kingdom now stands beneath the Iron Throne. If even the deserts could not halt the dragons, every unconquered ruler must weigh what remains of hope.

fab_ac_defender.1121.desc.text:
The last of Aegon Targaryen's banners has withdrawn from [ROOT.Char.GetPrimaryTitle.GetNameNoTier]. What the dragonlord proclaimed an inevitable conquest has broken against our armies, our strongholds, and the resolve of those who refused to kneel.

His dragons brought terror from the sky, but they could not occupy every road, guard every camp, or compel a kingdom to surrender after its people chose resistance. The conqueror departs with fewer soldiers and a legend diminished by defeat. Across Westeros, rulers who had begun to regard Aegon's triumph as destiny will hear a different tale now.

[ROOT.Char.GetHouse.GetName] stood before fire and blood—and endured. The dragon can be resisted. The dragon can be beaten.

fab_ac_defender.1121.a.text: Send word of this victory to every kingdom.

fab_ac_defender.demand.submit.text: I will spare my people. We submit.

fab_ac_defender.demand.fight.text: We will meet fire with steel.

ac_egg_quicksilver_desc.text: A silver egg. It will hatch #bold Quicksilver#!, the dragon of Aenys Targaryen. Give it to whichever child you want to ride it.

ac_egg_dreamfyre_desc.text: A pale blue egg. It will hatch #bold Dreamfyre#!, the dragon of Rhaena Targaryen. Give it to whichever child you want to ride it.

ac_egg_vermithor_desc.text: A bronze egg. It will hatch #bold Vermithor#!, the dragon of Jaehaerys Targaryen. Give it to whichever child you want to ride it.

ac_egg_cannibal_desc.text: A black egg. It will hatch #bold the Cannibal#!, a wild dragon of Dragonstone. Give it to whichever child you want to ride it.

ac_egg_silverwing_desc.text: A white egg. It will hatch #bold Silverwing#!, the dragon of Alysanne Targaryen. Give it to whichever child you want to ride it.

ac_egg_meleys_desc.text: A red egg. It will hatch #bold Meleys#!, called the Red Queen. Give it to whichever child you want to ride it.

fab_crowned_seven_desc.text: The Faith teaches that one god reveals seven faces: Father, Mother, Warrior, Maiden, Smith, Crone, and Stranger. Its worship is ordered through septs, septons, and the authority of the High Septon, with the Seven-Pointed Star at the heart of doctrine and devotion.

fab_deria_no_childbed_modifier_desc.text: The princess has no time for heirs while her house's fate hangs on her words. Dorne needs her living, not lying in.

fab_gulltown_blood_opinion.text: Blood in the Waters off Gulltown

fab_oldtown_scorched_modifier_desc.text: Oldtown bears the wounds of a long siege and dragonfire. Its broken streets, frightened people, and blackened holy places will require a generation to mend.

fab_ac_first_blood_modifier_desc.text: The first army raised against the dragons burned in a single afternoon, and Westeros has taken note.

fab_ac_reeds_bloodied_modifier_desc.text: The fighting on the Gods Eye shore was won, and the ranks it thinned will be slow to fill again.

fab_ac_wailing_willows_modifier_desc.text: A night raid out of the water gutted the baggage train and the rear guard. Replacements are slow in coming, and what is left costs more to keep in the field.

nick_fab_dragonsbane_desc.text: On a flooded field, in a storm that kept Meraxes on the ground, [CHARACTER.GetShortUINameNoTooltipNoFormat] rode forty horse at the dragon and drove a spear through her throat.

nick_fab_the_storm_queen_desc.text: Proclaimed on the walls of Storm's End in her dead father's crown, with Orys's host below and Meraxes across the bay.

ourfury.0001.desc.text:
The dragonlord's envoy stands before me in the great hall with Aegon's answer, and I make him give it before my lords. I offered Aegon Targaryen my daughter's hand and, as her dowry, the lands east of the Gods Eye between the Trident and the Blackwater, country the Storm Kings once held and Harren Hoare holds now. In return I asked for Dragonstone beside me when the time came to settle with Harren. There was sense in it. If Aegon wanted land, Harren had more than enough to lose, and I have never lacked the stomach to take it from him.

Aegon refuses the marriage. He has two wives already, both his sisters, and the heathen says he has no need of a third. Instead he offers his half-brother, Orys Waters, for Argella. The envoy calls him Aegon's companion and captain, as though command could put a father at a bastard's wedding or give him a name worth carving above a gate. Orys is baseborn, and Aegon proposes to put him in my daughter's bed.

That is not all. Aegon accepts the lands I named only as the beginning of the dowry. He also wants Massey's Hook and the Stormlander country running south from the Blackwater toward the Wendwater and the headwaters of the Mander. Those lands are mine already, held by men who have sworn before gods and men to Storm's End. I offered him Harren's hide, and the dragon has answered by reaching for mine.

There are men in this hall who would have the envoy thrown from the cliffs for less, and I do not blame them. Still, wrath is a poor reason to leave an enemy's meaning half heard. I will know the whole of Aegon's insolence before I decide what answer it deserves.

ourfury.0001.a.text: Guards. Take his hands. They are the only hands Aegon gets.

ourfury.0001.b.text: Say the whole of it. What else does the dragon offer?

ourfury.0001.c.text: Carry my refusal to Dragonstone. I have heard enough.

ourfury.0002.desc.text:
I let the envoy finish. Orys Waters is to wed Argella, and the lands east of the Gods Eye that I first named will pass with the marriage if we take them from Harren. Aegon also demands Massey's Hook and the country between the Blackwater, the Wendwater, and the upper Mander. In return, Dragonstone joins me against Harren Hoare. Aegon's strength will be turned north, not south, and neither king is asked to swear to the other.

That last part saves the offer from the privy. There is no demand for homage in Aegon's letter, no tribute, and no claim upon Storm's End. He wants land, a marriage, and a common war, and for all his heathen ways he has at least remembered that he is writing to a crowned king rather than summoning some petty lord to his hall.

Orys remains the difficulty. Argella is my only heir, and the man she marries will stand closer to Storm's End than any outsider has a right to stand. Yet the Seven did not decree that a wife's house must vanish into her husband's merely because scribes find the custom convenient. If Orys enters this house through Argella, then he enters it on my terms. The child who succeeds her can bear the name Durrandon, inherit Durrandon blood through his mother, and sit the seat his mother's fathers held before Dragonstone was more than a smoking rock.

Aegon may have the lands he asked for and the marriage he proposed. I will have his strength against Harren, and Storm's End will remain in my blood and under my name. If that is not enough for him, then he never wanted an alliance at all. #bold Orys Waters may marry my daughter, but the heir to Storm's End will be a Durrandon.#!

ourfury.0002.a.text: He weds into my house or not at all. Send that word.

ourfury.0002.b.text: No. A thousand years of Durrandons do not end in this hall.

ourfury.0003.desc.text:
The raven leaves Storm's End before dusk. I write the answer myself, because the matter is simple enough to fit in one line and important enough that I will not have a maester polish the edge off it.

#italic Your brother is welcome. His sons will be Durrandons.#!

My lords have objections, and none of them are shy about giving voice to them. Some object to Orys's birth, some to the lands Aegon has demanded, and some to any compact with a man who beds his own sisters and calls it marriage. I have heard them all. The Seven may judge Aegon's soul when they please; I am concerned with Harren Hoare, three dragons, and whether House Durrandon still sits Storm's End when the fighting is done.

I have conceded land rather than fight Harren and Dragonstone together, but I have conceded neither my crown nor my house. If Aegon accepts the condition, Orys comes south as Argella's husband and the pact stands. If he refuses it, he may keep his bastard and learn what the stormlands cost by another road. #bold The terms are sent. Dragonstone may take them or choke on them.#!

ourfury.0003.a.text: We will have Aegon's answer soon enough.

ourfury.0004.desc.text:
The answer from Dragonstone comes sooner than I expected, and Aegon accepts the condition without argument. Orys will come to Storm's End for the marriage, which will be made before my court and beneath the eyes of the Seven, and the children born to Argella will bear the Durrandon name and inherit through her.

The rest of the letter concerns the lands and the war. Massey's Hook and the country south of the Blackwater are to pass as agreed. When our banners move against Harren Hoare, Dragonstone will move with us. Aegon writes that he has no quarrel with a house that keeps faith with him and no wish to pull down an ancient line merely to prove that he can. Fine words from a man with three dragons, but I have heard worse terms from men with far less behind them.

I had expected haggling over the one condition I would not yield. Instead Aegon has accepted it at once, which means either that he understands the value of House Durrandon or that he is confident enough to let me keep my name while he takes what else he wants. I will discover which soon enough. #bold I asked for an ally against Harren. I have one, and I mean to see whether the dragon keeps faith as well as he writes it.#!

ourfury.0004.a.text: Open the gates to him. Storm's End fears no one bastard.

ourfury.0004.b.text: No. I will not marry my heir to Dragonstone after all.

ourfury.0005.desc.text:
They wed in the great hall beneath Durran's roof, before the Seven, the assembled storm lords, and enough witnesses that no man will later pretend he misunderstood the bargain. The septon names Argella Durrandon and Orys Waters before the Father and Mother, joins their hands, and calls upon the Seven to witness the vows. Aegon may make what excuses he pleases for wedding sister to brother on Dragonstone. In Storm's End, my daughter is wed according to the laws of gods and men.

Orys is not what some of my lords expected from a bastard of Dragonstone. He is broad, quiet, and careful with his courtesies. Men test him during the feast, as men will, and he gives none of them the quarrel they are looking for. I would almost prefer that he did, because a man's temper is easier to judge than his patience, but he repeats the terms of the marriage before the hall without hesitation. Argella's inheritance is hers, and the children who inherit through her will be Durrandons of Storm's End.

Argella has watched him closely since his arrival and has found more to say to him than she has said to me about the match. I will not call a handful of conversations affection, nor do I require it. Kings have married for poorer reasons than land, blood, and a useful sword, and many have done worse than a husband their daughter can bear to speak with. The marriage is lawful, the succession is settled, and the Seven have heard the vows. #bold Orys has entered House Durrandon. House Durrandon has not entered his.#!

ourfury.0005.a.text: Ours is the Fury, and no marriage changes that.

ourfury.0005.b.text: Pour the wine. The day has earned it.

ourfury.0006.desc.text:
The marriage settled one half of the bargain. Harren Hoare is the other. His monstrous castle rises beside the Gods Eye, and the riverlands he rules lie between my kingdom and the lands I promised to Argella's marriage. If those lands are ever to change hands, Harren must first be torn out of them, and I have wanted that ironborn blackguard humbled since long before Aegon Targaryen learned to look west.

The storm lords gather and ride north by the old roads through the kingswood and toward the Blackwater. Orys rides with them, and Aegon's banners are already moving from Dragonstone. I have no intention of wasting good stormland men against Harrenhal's walls if dragonfire can answer stone more cheaply, but castles are not kingdoms. Harren has riverlords, crossings, granaries, ferries, and armies that must be held while the dragons earn the land I have paid for.

So the storm rides with the dragon against the ironborn. I would have preferred a son of proper birth at my daughter's side and a smaller price for the alliance, but the bargain has been sworn and I keep my oaths, whatever liberties Aegon takes with the laws of gods and men in his own bed. #bold Sound the muster. Harren has sat on stolen lands long enough.#!

ourfury.0006.a.text: The storm rides north. Harren stole from us first.

ourfury.0006.b.text: Send my lords. A king need not ride every road himself.

ourfury.0007.desc.text:
Aegon Targaryen has come ashore at the mouth of the Blackwater, on the three hills where the fisherfolk beach their boats, and for the first time in my life a foreign host has landed within a few days' ride of my border without a stormlander reaching for a sword.

Massey's Hook is his. So is the country running south toward the Wendwater. I signed those lands away with my own hand and my own seal, which is a thing I have done for no man before, and there is no pretending they were taken from me. The lords who held them under Storm's End have new oaths to swear, and not one of them has sent me a complaint I would care to read aloud.

Riders came to these walls a year ago with word that dragons had been seen over the water, and men reached for their swords. Riders came again this morning with the same word, and it means the opposite. The beasts fly north once the muster is done. Harren Hoare spent forty years raising walls against an enemy worthy of them, and he will not wait much longer for one.

#bold The bargain is made. Now let the dragon prove he is worth what I paid for him.#!

ourfury.0007.a.text: The dragon is mine now. Harren will be the first to learn it.

ourfury.0010.desc.text:
The war has changed Westeros. Harren's grip on the riverlands is broken, and Aegon's ambitions have not ended with him. Reports from beyond my borders bring battles, bargains, submissions, and refusals, but none of them alters the agreement made here. The stormlands remain outside Aegon's rule, bound to him by marriage and treaty but not by oath, and I have no intention of allowing success elsewhere to make him forget the difference.

Aegon comes to Storm's End to speak of what follows. He confirms before I ask that Argella's children remain Durrandons and that the lands and rights already settled between us will stand. Then the heathen who once took care to write to me as one king to another asks for the one thing he left untouched.

He wants my crown. I am to surrender the kingship and remain Lord of Storm's End, with the stormlands, my vassals, my revenues, and my heirs left in my hands. I would rule the same country from the same seat, but beneath Aegon's crown instead of my own. Durran Godsgrief defied the gods themselves for this rock, and Aegon Targaryen now asks me to hand over what storms, ironmen, Andals, and Dornishmen all failed to take.

I know what war against his house would mean. I have seen the dragons at work, and only a fool mistakes knowing the strength of an enemy for fearing him. The question is whether I spend the lives of my lords and their sons to keep a circlet on my brow, or give Aegon his title and keep everything beneath it. #bold If I bend, it will be because I chose what House Durrandon could afford to lose, not because the heathen frightened me into it.#!

ourfury.0010.a.text: The crown is metal. Storm's End is stone, blood, and men.

ourfury.0010.b.text: Durran bent to no god. I will not bend to a heathen.

ourfury.0011.desc.text:
It is done in my own hall, before my own lords, because if I am to put down Durran's crown I will do it where every storm lord can see that no sword is at my throat. I place it in Aegon's hands myself. He receives it without triumph, sets it aside, and names me Lord of Storm's End, confirming the stormlands to me and my heirs beneath his crown.

Then my lords swear again. Yesterday their oaths ended with me. Today they pass through me to Aegon, but the men, castles, rents, judgments, and levies of the stormlands remain under the same hand. Argella is still my heir, and her children will still be Durrandons of Storm's End. Aegon has won a king's oath, not the right to unmake a thousand years of my house.

I was a king when the septon broke his fast this morning and I am not one now. I will not pretend that loss is nothing, nor will I grovel over it. Harren lost his lands, his line, and perhaps more besides. I have lost a crown and kept Storm's End, my daughter, my name, and every lord who mattered yesterday. Men may decide for themselves which bargain they would rather have made. #bold The crown is Aegon's. The storm remains Durrandon.#!

ourfury.0011.a.text: Ours is the Fury. King or lord, that much is mine.

ourfury.0020.desc.text:
I gave the envoy his answer before he had finished the offering of it, and I gave it standing, so that no man in the hall could mistake it for a thing still open to argument. Argella is not for sale to a bastard. Not for Harren's lands, not for Harren's head, and not for the friendship of a man who beds his own sisters and expects the Seven to look elsewhere.

Half my lords wanted him carried out in pieces. Fell said so plainly and Grandison said it louder. He went out through the gate on his own feet with his own hands, and that was not mercy. A king who cuts up heralds is a king no one troubles to send heralds to, and I have too many borders to spend that coin on one Valyrian's messenger. Aegon can have the refusal clean. He will not be able to tell it as the raving of an old man in a temper.

He will come south. I have expected it since the first raven flew to Dragonstone, and expecting it changes nothing. Ironborn, Andals, Dornishmen: every one of them came to this coast with better cause than a wedding refused, and every one of them went home short of men.

#bold He keeps his hands. He keeps his bastard. The rest we will settle in the field.#!

ourfury.0020.a.text: Send him home whole. The war comes either way.

ourfury.0021.text: The Whole of It, and No

ourfury.0021.desc.text:
I heard the whole of it. Every league of land, every clause, every courtesy. No homage asked, no tribute, no claim laid on Storm's End, and Dragonstone's strength turned north against Harren Hoare beside my own. I will not pretend it was a poor offer. It is better than any king in Westeros has been given by that family, and likely better than any will be.

It comes down to Argella all the same. She is my only child and the whole of my house after me, and Aegon proposes to settle her on a man with no name of his own and call the account balanced. A king may trade land. Land can be taken back, and I have taken some of it back twice in my life. What passes through a daughter passes once, and whatever is put in her bed sits in Durran's seat forever after.

So the answer is no, given whole and given knowing. No man will say afterward that I refused in anger without understanding what lay on the table. I understood it well enough. That is precisely why I would not have it.

#bold The dragon named a fair price. He asked for the one thing that was never for sale.#!

ourfury.0021.a.text: I have heard it all, and my answer stands.

ourfury.0022.desc.text:
Eleven days I have had Aegon's letter, and eleven days I have read it and set it down and taken it up again. He granted the condition without a word of argument. Argella's children will be Durrandons, he writes, as though it cost him nothing. I named that condition because I was certain it would break the whole business, and a man does not surrender so easily the thing he means to keep.

Either he does not care whose name is cut above the gate so long as the gate is his, or he means to have that too and reckons it can wait a generation. I have sat across a table from men who conceded everything and took it all back before the ink dried. I have been one of them.

The envoy is long gone and there is nobody left in this hall to shout at but my own lords, who told me what they thought when the first raven flew. So a second raven goes tonight and it takes the offer back. Aegon will have been generous where all Westeros could see it and refused where all Westeros could see that, and the tale will be told that way in every hall from here to the Wall. And so it will be told. I would sooner be called changeable than be called the king who put a bastard's line in Durran's seat and thanked him for the favour.

#bold I asked a price I thought he would not pay. He paid it, and that is what decided me.#!

ourfury.0022.a.text: Send the raven. The offer is withdrawn.

ourfury.0030.desc.text:
Aegon has declared for my crown, and there is no dressing this as an invasion. His brother sat at my table two winters ago and swore before the Seven that his sons would carry my name. The men marching out of Storm's End marched beside those banners at the Gods Eye. Some of them buried friends from that host and will now go looking for the ones who lived.

He wants the circlet and nothing beside it. Not Storm's End, not the stormlands, not Argella's inheritance. He has asked for none of them and he will get none of them by asking. Only the crown of Durran Godsgrief, and only because a realm with two kings in it is not yet the realm he says he has.

Orys will come south. Aegon has sent Orys for the stormlands from the beginning and sees no reason to stop now. My own goodson against my own banners, and whatever grandsons the gods see fit to give me will hear about it from whichever side is left to do the telling.

#bold I kept every oath I swore to that house. I never swore them this one.#!

ourfury.0030.a.text: Call the banners. The crown was never his to ask for.

ourfury.0030.b.text: He is my daughter's husband. He will swear it.

ourfury.0030.c.text: Send him back to his brother.

ourfury.0030.d.text: Take him. He'll not command my men.

ourfury.0033.desc.text:
I have him brought into the great hall with every storm lord in Storm's End standing to watch it, because a thing done quietly is a thing that can be argued about later. Orys Waters is my daughter's husband, my grandsons will carry my name, and his brother's host is marching down my roads. Two of those three are worth something to me. I mean to find out which.

He does not make me ask twice. He goes down on one knee on the stones in front of the whole hall, and he says it plainly and without ornament: that he is sworn to Storm's End and to the house he married into, that Aegon released him of nothing when he sent him south, and that he will draw his sword for me against any man living. He does not say his brother's name. I notice that he does not, and I let it pass.

Argella watches from the dais and does not look at me once. She has more to lose here than either of us and she knows exactly what I would have done to him if he had hesitated. He did not hesitate. Whatever else the Seven made him, they did not make him a coward, and I have known a great many highborn men who were.

So he rides with us. Men will say I was a fool to allow it and those men are welcome to say so where I can hear them. I have taken oaths from better-born men who kept them worse.

#bold He knelt in my hall and swore before the Seven. Now let the dragon come and see what he bought with that bastard.#!

ourfury.0033.a.text: Rise, goodson. You ride on my right hand.

ourfury.0031.desc.text:
The terms are signed and I keep the crown. Aegon has not lost his realm and I will insult neither of us by claiming he has. He has lost a war he chose to begin, and he has paid for it in the only coin I wanted.

Massey's Hook is Durrandon ground again. So is the Wendwater forest and the woods along the Baywater, which means every holding south of that new town of his sends its levies to Storm's End now. The Storm Kings held all of it before a Targaryen ever crossed the water, and I have held it twice in one lifetime, which is more than most men manage with anything.

There is less satisfaction in it than I expected. Orys is still my goodson and Argella is still his wife, and there are storm lords in the ground who rode under the dragon's banners before they rode against them. A war won is a war won. It is not the same thing as never having needed one.

#bold He came for the crown of Durran Godsgrief and went home with less than he brought.#!

ourfury.0031.a.text: The Hook answers to Storm's End again.

ourfury.0032.desc.text:
The terms Aegon sets are the terms he set before a single man died. My crown for my lands. Storm's End, the stormlands, my lords, my revenues, and Argella after me, all of it kept and all of it held beneath his. Not one word has moved. He did not need to move it.

So I have bought with a war exactly what I was offered for nothing, and all I have to show for the difference is the certainty that I could not have won it. I told my lords I would not be frightened into kneeling, and I was not. I was beaten into it. The singers may find that prettier. I do not.

The worst of it is not Aegon. Aegon is a conqueror and conquerors take crowns, and there is no great shame in losing to a man who has taken six of them. The worst of it is that his brother sits at my table on feast days, wed to my daughter, and that the men who broke my host will be drinking in my hall before the year is out.

#bold I would not sell the crown. In the end I gave it away and paid for the privilege.#!

ourfury.0032.a.text: Take it, then. It cost me a war to learn its price.

ourfury.0100.desc.text:
So it is war. I have rejected Dragonstone and called my banners, and the storm lords have answered as storm lords should. Fell comes from Felwood, Errol from Haystack Hall, Buckler from Bronzegate, Grandison from Grandview, and Dondarrion down from Blackhaven with every marcher sword he can spare. Aegon may call himself whatever he pleases on his rock. South of the Blackwater, men still answer to Argilac Durrandon.

The rains have come early and hard. Roads that were firm a fortnight ago are mud from the Blackwater south, and every stream is running high. The Seven have sent me weather fit for a Storm King. A dragon can cross country that would stop an army, but Orys still needs wagons, fodder, dry bowstrings, and ground on which men can stand.

Orys is marching south with the greater part of Aegon's host, and Rhaenys Targaryen is with him on Meraxes. I have more men, better knowledge of the country, and lords defending their own fields. He has a dragon. I do not need to pretend that last advantage is small, but neither will I behave as though one beast has already conquered the stormlands. Where we meet will decide whether Orys learns that himself.

ourfury.0100.a.text: The kingswood. He will learn what my trees conceal.

ourfury.0100.b.text: The open field. No hedges, no tricks, no excuses.

ourfury.0100.c.text: The Rainwood. Orys can drown in it first.

ourfury.0110.desc.text:
Fell, Buckler, and Errol struck the Targaryen van as it crossed the Wendwater. They came out of the trees at first light, killed men before Orys could bring the rest of his host into order, and withdrew before the weight of his army could close around them. By midday a great many of his men were dead or missing, and the storm lords had disappeared back into country they have hunted, ridden, and bled over since boyhood.

Rhaenys brought Meraxes up before midday, but low cloud, driving rain, and the tree cover kept her from finding the raiders in force. She burned stretches of woodland along the road and forced the storm lords farther back, but most had already scattered before the dragon reached them. I am told some of Orys's men cheered when she came overhead. Men cheer loudly when they need reminding that they are not afraid.

The ambush has cost Orys blood and time, and it has shown us how quickly Meraxes can punish a mistake. Good. I would rather know the beast's reach now than discover it with half my host trapped beneath her. #bold Orys has entered my country. He will pay for every road, ford, and stand of trees he takes from me.#!

ourfury.0110.a.text: Keep cutting. Give the bastard no peaceful mile.

ourfury.0110.b.text: Enough small fighting. Draw him toward a battle line.

ourfury.0111.desc.text:
News of the fighting has travelled beyond the stormlands. Merchants and envoys bring questions about the Wendwater and about Meraxes being checked by the weather. The rest of Westeros can gossip. The only judgment that concerns me is inside my own camp, where men who once looked skyward at every shadow have now seen dragon men bleed like any others.

My lords have watched Orys lose men on roads he does not know. They have watched Meraxes forced low by rain and wind. Their confidence has returned, and I mean to use it before caution grows back into fear. A lord may be forgiven for respecting a dragon. He will not be forgiven for teaching his men to fear one before it appears.

Orys still has a disciplined host, and Rhaenys still has Meraxes. I know that as well as any trembling maester who can add one dragon to one army and declare the sum unbeatable. #bold We have bloodied them once. By the Warrior, I mean to do it again before they remember their courage.#!

ourfury.0111.a.text: Ride with the van. I will not shelter behind my lords.

ourfury.0111.b.text: Hold the line. Prudence is not fear.

ourfury.0112.desc.text:
The gale has settled over the coast and has not eased for three days. Meraxes remains on the ground above the Wendwater with her wings folded tight against the rain. My scouts have seen Rhaenys try to take her up twice, and both attempts ended almost as soon as they began. If the Seven mean to hand me a dragon chained by weather, I will not insult them by refusing the gift.

Without Meraxes in the air, Orys has to move as any other commander does. His host is smaller than mine, deep in country that answers to Storm's End, and forced onto roads the rain has reduced to mud. He may be Aegon's Hand, brother, bastard, or all three together. On the ground he is still a man leading men, and I have beaten better men than him.

The weather will not hold forever. When the wind drops, Rhaenys will rise again and every advantage changes with her. Until then the field belongs to soldiers, and no one south of the Blackwater has more right to it than I do. #bold While Meraxes is grounded, Orys will learn what became of every man who mistook the stormlands for easy country.#!

ourfury.0112.a.text: March. The Warrior has given us our hour.

ourfury.0112.b.text: Send scouts. I want to know whether men could reach her.

ourfury.0120.desc.text:
The wind eased before dawn, and Rhaenys wasted no time. Meraxes took the air low over the trees and found the storm lords who had been troubling Orys's march since the Wendwater. The rain had soaked the forest for days, but dragonfire burned through wet leaves, green branches, horses, and men alike. The Stranger took his due quickly once she found them.

Lord Errol is dead. Fell and Buckler brought back what they could of their commands, many without shields or horses, and every man among them reeks of smoke. They speak less of the men they lost than of the sound Meraxes made above the trees before the fire came down. I will not call them cravens for it. A craven runs before the danger arrives. These men stood until the sky itself burned them out.

I can replace horses. I cannot replace lords, and I will not keep feeding good men into woods that Meraxes can turn into a furnace merely to prove I possess courage. Anyone who mistakes prudence for fear may say so in my hearing. #bold The dragon is flying again. We change the war before she changes it for us.#!

ourfury.0120.a.text: Scatter the host. The beast can hunt shadows.

ourfury.0120.b.text: Hold together. Every bow we have will be waiting for her.

ourfury.0121.desc.text:
Three lords came to my tent tonight, and none of them came only for himself. Grandison spoke for the rest. Errol is dead, Fell has lost near half the men he took north, Buckler is short of horses, and every raven from the coast brings another account of villages emptying before the Targaryen advance. No man in the tent used the word fear. They are storm lords, and they have earned better than that from me.

Then Grandison told me Aegon's terms are being repeated openly through Orys's camp. Any storm lord who bends the knee keeps his lands, his castle, and his name. The heathen has learned enough of Westeros to know where to place the knife. He is not asking my lords to betray their homes. He is offering to spare those homes if they betray me.

Grandison did not ask leave to desert. He said that if I commanded him to remain, his house would remain and take whatever came with it. By the Seven, that is why the decision is mine rather than his. Their oaths give me the right to demand everything. A king who spends brave men merely because they are brave enough to obey him has mistaken pride for duty. #bold I will decide what loyalty to House Durrandon requires, and no dragonlord will decide it for me.#!

ourfury.0121.a.text: Hold them to their oaths. None leaves while I stand.

ourfury.0121.b.text: Cravens and oathbreakers. They can run home to their walls.

ourfury.0122.desc.text:
Bronzegate is taken, my army has been forced back across the Slayne, and I have perhaps eleven thousand men left of the twenty thousand who answered the first muster. The right gave way at the ford after Meraxes made repeated passes over it. Those men were not cravens. I saw horses burning beneath them and men trying to close ranks while their shields caught fire. The Warrior himself could ask no more of mortal men. Buckler died holding them together long enough for the rest to cross.

The road to Storm's End lies open behind me. I have sent Argella back with orders to prepare the castle and keep the garrison steady. She knows as well as I do that walls alone will not win this war while Meraxes can fly, but Storm's End has outlived every fool who thought stone was all that held it.

I still have an army, and Orys has not destroyed it. If I continue yielding ground, there will soon be no ground left between him and my daughter's inheritance. I can choose the next field, bring every man I have left onto it, and force this war to a decision before Meraxes burns the kingdom apart by pieces. I have retreated far enough for any man who ever means to call me craven. #bold The next ground I give Orys will be measured in blood, not miles.#!

ourfury.0122.a.text: Turn and fight. No man will call Argilac Durrandon craven.

ourfury.0122.b.text: Fall back to Storm's End. The walls have never failed us.

ourfury.0130.desc.text:
Orys has taken the hills south of Bronzegate and dug his men into the high ground. In clear weather I would call it a strong position and let him grow hungry on it. The weather is anything but clear. Rain is driving across the field hard enough to blind a bowman, the slopes are turning to mud, and Meraxes is crouched on the hillside with Rhaenys beside her, unable to stay aloft in the gale. The gods have sent me a storm fit for the name Durrandon.

My host is larger, and the gale has taken away much of the advantage that brought Orys this far. It has not taken away the hill. We will have to climb for him, and every horse that loses its footing will open a gap for his spears. So be it. The Warrior does not promise dry ground, and neither do I.

I ride the line before we begin. Fell is there, Grandison is there, Dondarrion and Morrigen and what remains of Buckler's men are there. They have followed me through every retreat of this campaign and have not yet refused an order. I will not ask such men to spend another day wondering whether their king still has the courage to use them. #bold Sound the charge. If Orys wants the stormlands, he can take them from us here.#!

ourfury.0130.a.text: Drive at the center. Break him where he feels strongest.

ourfury.0130.b.text: Take the left slope. I will have his hill from under him.

ourfury.0131.desc.text:
The first charge died on the slope. The second reached the Targaryen line and was thrown back in the mud. On the third we broke into their center, and for a time there was no line at all, only stormland horse forcing uphill through rain while Orys's foot tried to close the gap. I have heard men call cavalry useless in mud. Those men have never ridden with mine.

Then Meraxes found room to breathe fire. She could not take the sky, but she did not need to. The front of my vanguard vanished behind flame, and horses that had carried knights through three charges tore free of their riders and ran. My own horse went down beneath me in the crush. By the time I got clear, my shield arm was numb and the battle had closed around us on foot. If the Stranger wants me, he will have to come into the mud for me.

The storm lords are still fighting. Every time Orys's men push into the breach, another knot of household knights meets them and the center holds a little longer. Somewhere above the rain a horn is sounding from the hill, and men ahead of me are moving aside for someone coming down through their ranks. I know who it is before I see him. #bold Good. I have had enough of killing men sent by Orys Waters. He may answer for his own war now.#!

ourfury.0131.a.text: I will meet him. A Storm King does not hide.

ourfury.0132.text: The Bastard Comes Down the Hill

ourfury.0132.desc.text:
Orys Waters stops a few paces from me in the mud and calls on me to yield. He gives me my titles, offers quarter to the men still fighting around us, and says that if I lay down my sword I will keep Storm's End, Argella will keep her inheritance, and the storm lords who submit with me will keep their lands. He speaks as though these things are already his to give back to me.

He is younger, unwounded, and armoured to the throat. I have lost my horse and shield, my left hand barely closes, and there are Targaryen men behind him on the hill. I grant him every advantage and not one right to command me. A man does not become my king because he stands on higher ground, and a bastard does not become generous by offering me my own castle.

#italic Yield, Your Grace.#!

Durrandons have been driven from fields before. We have been besieged, beaten, starved, and forced to buy peace, and still Storm's End bears our name. I will not be the first of my line to discover cowardice because Orys Waters asks politely enough. #bold If he wants the sword of the Storm King, he may come and take it.#!

ourfury.0132.desc.courtesy.text:
Orys Waters stops a few paces from me and removes his helm before he speaks. Whatever else I think of the man, that much is properly done. He gives terms face to face while men are still dying around us, and he gives me every title that Aegon's camp has spent this war trying to take away.

He offers quarter to the storm lords if I yield. Storm's End remains with my house, Argella's inheritance is confirmed, and my vassals keep their lands. He even offers me a place at his own table after the war, which sounds like more than his heathen brother instructed him to promise and perhaps is. I can respect the courage it takes to make such an offer without pretending I am obliged to accept it.

#italic Yield, Your Grace. Please.#!

For a moment I understand why Aegon trusts him. Then I look past Orys at the men still fighting under my banner and at the crowned stag hanging wet above them. Courtesy deserves courtesy, not surrender. #bold I will answer him as one warrior answers another. If he wants my submission, he must win it with steel.#!

ourfury.0132.a.text: Give him his answer with steel.

ourfury.0132.b.text: Cut me a road out. They may say what they like of it.

ourfury.0135.desc.text:
Orys Waters is dead in the mud at my feet, and the men around us know it before I do. He was stronger than I expected and quicker than a man his size had any right to be. Early in the fight he put his sword through my left shoulder, and after that I had no strength to waste. I gave ground, kept him turning in the mud, and waited until he committed too much weight to a cut he thought would end it. There is no shame in admitting the bastard was good. He is dead all the same.

I remember the opening more clearly than the stroke that followed. His footing went, my blade found him beneath the arm, and the man who had marched south to take Storm's End went to his knees before me. By the time my household knights reached us, the cry had spread through both lines and Orys's center was beginning to pull back from the hill. The Warrior may judge which of us fought better. The field has already given its judgment.
