They get me onto another horse and bind the shoulder as best they can. Then I see Meraxes across the field, still grounded by the gale, with Rhaenys beside her and the remnants of Orys's host between us. I have killed Aegon's Hand. The gods have left one of his dragons sitting in the mud within sight of my banner. A cautious man would call that victory enough. #bold I have never been accused of being a cautious man. If Meraxes can be reached, I mean to reach her.#!

ourfury.0135.a.text: Forty horse with me. Let us see whether dragons bleed.

ourfury.0135.b.text: Sound the recall. I will not turn victory into vanity.

ourfury.0136.text: The Day the Storm Broke Them

ourfury.0136.desc.text:
I watched Meraxes on the hillside while my lords pulled the army back into order. For a time I wanted every horse that could still move sent across the field after her. Fell finally put a hand on my bridle, which very few men in Westeros would dare, and told me what I already knew: Orys was dead, his center was retreating, and my own men were too spent to survive another charge if the dragon turned on them.

So I sounded the recall. I do not like retreating from any living thing, least of all a wounded dragon, but there is a difference between courage and throwing away men who have already won my battle for me. Some court fool may call that caution craven if he wishes. He may come to Storm's End and explain it before the same lords who stood with me in the mud.

Meraxes still lives and Aegon still has wars to make, but Orys came south to break my kingdom and lies dead on the field he chose. My shoulder will not rise much above my chest, yet I am alive, my army is still mine, and Storm's End remains behind us. #bold The bastard came for my crown. The Stranger has him instead.#!

ourfury.0136.a.text: Bind the wound. I am not finished with Aegon yet.

ourfury.0140.desc.text:
I take forty horse across the flooded field toward Meraxes. More men would slow us and draw attention sooner. Fewer would leave us no hope of reaching her through the guards gathering around Rhaenys. Some men will call this madness if any of them live long enough to hear of it. I have been called worse things by better men. The rain is so heavy that the dragon disappears between one heartbeat and the next, then returns larger each time the distance closes.

At close range there is nothing graceful about her. Meraxes fills the hillside with folded wing, pale scale, muscle, and the heat of her breath. Her head alone is larger than a warhorse's chest, and one eye follows us as we approach. I had expected size and fire. I had not expected the certainty that there was thought behind that eye, or that the beast would look at me as though I were the one who had trespassed.

Rhaenys is at the base of the neck, shouting commands in the Valyrian tongue and trying to get the dragon upright. Meraxes shifts her weight and the men around me lower their spears without being told. I commend my soul to the Seven, set the spear beneath my arm, and choose the narrow place where throat meets breast. #bold If the Warrior has carried me this far, he may watch what comes next.#!

ourfury.0140.a.text: Ride. Forty horse will learn whether a dragon can be killed.

ourfury.0141.desc.text:
Eleven men return to Storm's End from the forty who rode with my father, and the account they give agrees in the parts that matter. They reached Meraxes before the dragon could take flight. She rose onto her forelegs instead, and one sweep of a folded wing broke the left side of the charge before she ever opened her mouth.

My father passed the wing. Two men saw his spear strike at the base of the neck and saw the point go in. Then Rhaenys gained the saddle, Meraxes turned her head, and the fire took horse and rider together. None of the eleven saw him rise again.

He had removed his crown before the charge and given it to a squire. That is what has come back to me, along with his surviving men and the knowledge that the field is lost to us. #bold My father is dead. His crown is on my table, and Storm's End is mine to hold.#!

ourfury.0142.desc.text:
My spear went in at the base of Meraxes's throat where the scales narrowed against the neck. I felt the shaft drive deeper than I thought any spear could go, then the dragon twisted and nearly tore my arm from its socket. Men and horses vanished beneath her wing as she came around, but the wound kept pouring dark blood into the rain. So dragons bleed after all, and by the Seven there is a great deal of it.

I remember very little in order after that. Fell's nephew was taken by the wing beside me. Someone pulled Rhaenys clear when Meraxes lurched onto her side. The dragon tried twice to rise and could not. Each movement grew weaker until the great neck settled into the mud and did not lift again. Men who had spent the whole war fearing the sound of her wings stood around her in silence and watched the life go out of her.

Orys was already dead, and the sight of Meraxes falling finished what remained of his army. His men broke north toward the Blackwater, carrying Rhaenys with them. She was alive when they took her from the field, though badly hurt. I had neither the horses nor the strength left to pursue far, and I will not apologize for failing to chase beaten men after killing their commander and their dragon in the same field.

Meraxes lies where she fell, so large even in death that men lower their voices beside her. Aegon Targaryen may keep his sister-wives, his heathen customs, and whatever titles he has gathered elsewhere. One of the dragons with which he crossed the Blackwater is dead in my kingdom, and the crowned stag still flies above Storm's End. #bold The heathen will hear that plainly. The stormlands are not his.#!

ourfury.0142.a.text: Send the news. I want Aegon to hear who killed his dragon.

ourfury.0150.desc.text:
Orys Waters beat me in the mud before two armies, and there is no lie worth telling about it. He was younger, he was stronger, and he kept his feet at the end of a long day when I could not. When I went down his sword was already through me.

So I lie here in the mud and the guts and the blood, which is how it ends for a soldier, and I have never claimed to be anything else. Fifty years of war, and the ground was always waiting.

Aegon can have the field. He cannot have the last of it.

#bold I am Argilac Durrandon, and I will live forever in the songs.#!

ourfury.0150.a.text: So dies the last of the Storm Kings.

ourfury.0160.desc.text:
My father is dead, and before the day is out I have myself proclaimed Queen of the Stormlands from the walls of Storm's End. The garrison sees the crown on my head, the captains swear before the same men they command, and every gate is barred before nightfall.

Storm's End has withstood storms, sieges, and wars since Durran raised the seventh castle on this cliff. I have four hundred men within the walls, provisions enough to endure a long investment, and a fortress no ordinary army can take by assault. Across the bay, however, Rhaenys and Meraxes are with the force that killed my father, and no wall can make a dragon fight by the rules of an ordinary siege.

The crown will not stop Meraxes. It can keep the question clear. If Orys wants the stormlands, he must deal with the woman who inherited them, and my own men must decide whether they will hold Storm's End with me before the enemy decides it for them. #bold My father is gone. House Durrandon is not.#!

ourfury.0160.a.text: Bar the gates. Man the walls.

ourfury.0160.b.text: Send to Orys under a peace banner. Him, not his brother.

ourfury.0160.b.other.text: Send to [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] under a peace banner. No one else is left to treat with.

ourfury.0160.a.hold.text: Bar the gates. My men will hold them.

ourfury.0160.a.yield.text: You. Put that down and step away from the door.

ourfury.0160.desc.noorys.text:
My father is dead, and before the day is out I have myself proclaimed Queen of the Stormlands from the walls of Storm's End. The garrison sees the crown on my head, the captains swear before the same men they command, and every gate is barred before nightfall.

Orys Waters is dead as well. My father killed him in the mud in front of two armies, and so the bastard Aegon meant to seat in this castle will never see the inside of it. Whatever else my father spent, and he spent all of it, he bought that.

What is left across the bay is [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName], a dragon, and a host that has lost the man who was leading it. I have four hundred men, provisions enough for a long investment, and a fortress no ordinary army takes by assault. None of that is an argument against a dragon. It is only what I have.

#bold My father is gone, and so is the man they meant me for. House Durrandon is neither.#!

ourfury.0310.desc.text:
[fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] has been camped beneath these walls long enough that the men have stopped using tents and started calling the place by a name. There has been no assault. Storm's End has never been taken by assault, and nobody down there is fool enough to want to be the first to try.

I have four hundred men. I had four hundred when I put my father's crown on my head and I have four hundred still, which sounds like steadiness until you count how many of them have wives and fields in the villages that host is feeding. Nobody has opened a gate. That is not the same thing as nobody thinking about it.

Meraxes is close enough that I can see her from the seaward wall, and I look for her every morning before I have decided to. Durran's descendants have been told all our lives that a wall standing a thousand years will stand another winter. None of them ever had to explain a wall to a dragon.

#bold The gates hold as long as I say they hold. I would dearly like to know how long that will be true.#!

ourfury.0310.a.text: The gates hold. He can sit in the mud.

ourfury.0310.a.hold.text: The gates hold, and my captains hold with them.

ourfury.0310.b.yield.text: So it is tonight, and it is my own men.

ourfury.0310.c.text: Send to Orys. I will treat with him before they treat for me.

ourfury.0310.c.other.text: Send to [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName]. I will treat before my captains treat for me.

ourfury.0310.desc.nodragon.text:
[fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] has been camped beneath these walls long enough that the men have stopped using tents and started calling the place by a name. There has been no assault. Storm's End has never been taken by assault, and nobody down there is fool enough to want to be the first to try.

I have four hundred men. I had four hundred when I put my father's crown on my head and I have four hundred still, which sounds like steadiness until you count how many of them have wives and fields in the villages that host is feeding. Nobody has opened a gate. That is not the same thing as nobody thinking about it.

There is no dragon over the bay. That is the one thing in this siege that has gone as no one expected, and I have watched men on the walls look up at an empty sky and stand a little straighter for it. An empty sky does not feed four hundred men, but I will take what the Seven send.

#bold The gates hold as long as I say they hold. I would dearly like to know how long that will be true.#!

ourfury.0320.desc.delivered.text:
They came for me at night, and I will give them that much credit, because it meant they were ashamed. Four of my own captains, men who swore to me in this hall with my father three days in the ground. They took my sword first and the crown second and neither of them looked at me while they did it.

They carried me to Orys Waters bound and stripped and gagged, and they made a present of me, the way a man makes a present of plate or a horse or the keys to a gate. I have thought a great deal since about which of those they had in mind. I have settled on the keys.

Orys had them whipped. He did not thank them, he did not pay them, and he had me cut loose and covered before he would hear one word from anyone in that tent. Whatever else may be true of the man, he knew exactly what had been done and he wanted no share in the doing of it.

#bold Storm's End was not taken. It was sold, by men who could not have told you what they were selling.#!

ourfury.0320.desc.parley.text:
I sent to [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] under a peace banner and I walked out of my own gate to meet them, which is more than my father would have done and more than half my captains expected. There was no rope and nobody carried me. Whatever gets written about this afterward, that part belongs to me.

The terms are what they were always going to be. Storm's End, the stormlands, and the crown of Durran Godsgrief, all of it into Targaryen hands. Walking out standing bought me nothing at the table. It bought me walking out standing.

My captains are relieved and working hard not to show it, and I have decided not to hold that against them. Four hundred men against a host and a dragon was never a wall. It was a number I said out loud to see whether saying it would make it so.

#bold I gave it away. That is not the same as having it taken, and I intend to be the one who remembers the difference.#!

ourfury.0320.desc.beaten.text:
It is finished, and it finished in the field rather than at these gates, which is the only mercy anywhere in it. The stormlands are spent. There are no musters left to call, no lords left with men to send, and no road in this kingdom the Targaryens have not walked down at their leisure.

I held Storm's End. That is the entire account of what I can say for myself. The walls never opened, the garrison never broke, and none of it mattered, because a kingdom is not a castle, and I ran out of the one while I was busy keeping the other.

Aegon's terms come south with [fab_ourfury_foe.GetTitledFirstName] and they are not cruel. They were never going to need to be. A man does not have to be cruel to a woman who has nothing left in her hands to take.

#bold I kept the gate and lost the kingdom. My father would have understood that arithmetic and hated it exactly as much as I do.#!

ourfury.0320.a.text: So it ends. Let me hear the terms.

ourfury.0320.desc.beaten.noorys.text:
It is finished, and it finished in the field rather than at these gates, which is the only mercy anywhere in it. The stormlands are spent. There are no musters left to call, no lords left with men to send, and no road in this kingdom the Targaryens have not walked down at their leisure.

I held Storm's End. That is the entire account of what I can say for myself. The walls never opened, the garrison never broke, and none of it mattered, because a kingdom is not a castle, and I ran out of the one while I was busy keeping the other.

Aegon's terms arrive without the man who was meant to bring them. My father saw to that much. It has made no difference to a single line of them and I never thought it would, but I find I am glad of it anyway, and I have stopped apologising to myself for being glad.

#bold I kept the gate and lost the kingdom. My father would have understood that arithmetic and hated it exactly as much as I do.#!

ourfury.0321.text: A Cloak, and a Name Not Mine

ourfury.0321.desc.text:
Orys Waters is to have Storm's End, and me along with it. Aegon has settled the matter the way he settles everything now, which is briefly and in writing, and there is nobody left standing in Westeros in a position to tell him otherwise.

He is not the creature my father described. My father made him out to be a stain, a bastard offered as an insult, and answered him with a box. I have watched the man for a fortnight and he is quiet, careful, unhandsome, and visibly uncomfortable with having won. That is worse in its way. It would be far easier if he were what I was promised.

He asked me rather than told me, which nothing required of him, and which I noticed. The answer is the same either way and we both know it. But he asked, and I will remember that he asked, and one day the singers will want to know which of those two things was the marriage.

#bold I am the last of Durran's line and the first of whatever this is. Ours is the fury still. It will simply fly under a different beast.#!

ourfury.0321.desc.delivered.text:
He put his own cloak on me before he asked me anything at all, and he did it himself, and he did it standing in front of the men who had brought me. That is the first thing I will say about Orys Waters and I have decided it is the thing I will keep saying, because the rest of that night belongs to me and I do not intend to hand it to singers.

He is to have Storm's End by Aegon's word, and me with it. I could tell you I was given no choice, and it would be true, and it would also be the smaller half of the truth. He asked. He asked after everything that had already been done to me, when not one man alive would have made him, and he waited for an answer he had no need of.

My father would have refused him. My father did refuse him, with a box, and that box is most of the reason I am standing in another man's cloak watching my house end behind me. I have thought about that a great deal and I am not sure I have finished.

#bold He covered me when my own men would not. It is a thin thing to build a marriage on. It is more than my father left me.#!

ourfury.0321.desc.noorys.text:
Orys Waters is dead, killed by my father in the mud in front of two armies, and the marriage Aegon designed for me died in the same place. There is no bastard left to hand me to and no cloak coming for my shoulders.

Aegon's terms stand regardless. The stormlands are his, the crown of Durran Godsgrief is his, and I hold Storm's End at his pleasure rather than by any right of my blood. What he has not done is find me another husband, and I have no intention of reminding him that the thought is available to him.

So I am the Durrandon who kept the seat and lost everything above it. Unmarried, unpromised, and for the moment unspoken for. My father would call that a poor bargain. My father is also dead, and the last thing he did on this earth was make certain the man meant to have me never would.

#bold He is gone, and Orys is gone, and I am still here. That will have to serve for now.#!

ourfury.0321.a.text: Give me the cloak. I know what it costs.

ourfury.0321.b.text: Then I remain Durrandon, whatever else is lost.

ourfury.0170.desc.text:
It is finished, and I am alive to see the terms written. Aegon's answer comes after Orys's victory, formal and almost painfully restrained. He demands my crown and my oath, but he does not demand Storm's End, Argella's inheritance, or the destruction of my house. Courtesy in defeat is difficult to stomach, but it leaves a man fewer excuses for refusing to hear what is being offered.

I surrender the crown of Durran Godsgrief and acknowledge Aegon as king. In return I remain Lord of Storm's End, holding the stormlands from the Marches to Tarth beneath Aegon's crown, with the revenues and rights of my house and the fealty of the lords who have sworn to the Durrandons. Argella remains my unquestioned heir.

I ask what becomes of the marriage he once proposed. Aegon's answer is that Orys will be rewarded elsewhere and that he has no intention of using Argella's hand as a second price for lands I have already surrendered by oath. Whatever else may be said of him, he does not press the advantage beyond the terms he needs.

I am the Durrandon who put down the crown, and that name will follow me. It will also follow Argella into Storm's End after I am gone. The kingship ends here, but the house does not. #bold I have lost a crown and kept the inheritance beneath it.#!

ourfury.0170.a.text: So be it. Storm's End remains Durrandon.

ourfury.0200.desc.text:
Aegon's army has withdrawn from the stormlands. The men who followed Orys south are gone from our roads, their camps stand empty, and no dragon circles above the marches. I do not know where Aegon will turn next, and I have no intention of sitting in Storm's End inventing victories for him that he has not won.

The war has changed Westeros. Aegon's claims have not gone unanswered elsewhere, and every court has made its own choices while we fought. They can keep their own accounts. Mine is simple enough: Aegon sent an army into the stormlands, and that army went back without my crown. Whatever banners now fly beyond my borders, the crowned stag still flies here.

We have not restored the world that existed before the dragons crossed the Blackwater, nor could we. The Seven alone know what the next ravens will bring. For now, Storm's End is still mine, my lords still answer my summons, and no foreign king holds my oath. #bold Aegon may call himself conqueror where men have bent to him. In the stormlands he may call himself repulsed.#!

ourfury.0200.a.text: Send the news to every court, and in my own words.

ourfury.0200.desc.argella.text:
Aegon's army has withdrawn from the stormlands. Orys is gone from our roads, the camps below the walls are pits full of rainwater, and no dragon has been seen above the marches in a month.

I was proclaimed on these walls with my father three days dead and a host in the fields below, and there were captains in this hall who did the arithmetic out loud in front of me. Four hundred men. One dragon across the bay. A girl of twenty in a dead man's crown. I kept a list of who said what. I have not yet decided what the list is for.

The war has changed Westeros and I will not pretend the stormlands changed it alone. Kings have knelt elsewhere and made their own bargains and must live in them. Mine is simpler than any of theirs. Aegon Targaryen sent an army for my crown and the army went home without it.

#bold They believed they were burying House Durrandon. They were watching it change hands.#!

ourfury.0201.desc.text:
The ravens begin before the field has dried. Some come from kings, some from lords, and some from men careful not to put a title at the top of the page. There are congratulations among them, but more questions. They want to know how Orys was beaten, what became of Meraxes, how badly Aegon's host was hurt, and whether Storm's End expects him to return. Men who would not have wagered a clipped copper on me before the battle have suddenly discovered great respect for the stormlands.

Offers come mixed with the questions. Grain, horses, envoys, marriages, ships, and promises of mutual defense are all put before me, though their worth will depend entirely on who still keeps his word when the next army moves. I take none of it for friendship. The Father may judge sincerity; a king is better served judging what another man can actually deliver.

What matters is that every court now understands that Aegon's will is not the same thing as fate. I know better than any of them what the victory cost and how much the weather favored us, but I also know whose men stood in that weather and whose sword killed Orys Waters. #bold I will hear every offer, and I will bargain from the seat Aegon failed to take from me.#!

ourfury.0201.a.text: Answer every court. Make them wait on my words.

ourfury.0201.b.text: The men with ships first. Compliments garrison nothing.

ourfury.0201.desc.argella.text:
The ravens start before the ground has dried. Congratulations mostly, with questions underneath them. They want to know how the siege was broken, what became of Meraxes, how badly Orys was hurt, and whether Storm's End expects him back. Men who would not have wagered a clipped copper on me have discovered a sudden and enormous respect for the stormlands.

A great many of them want to know who I mean to marry. Two have proposed themselves. One has proposed his son, who is eleven. I am reading these letters slowly and answering none of them quickly, because a queen in a hurry to be married is a queen who has told the world exactly what she thinks she is worth.

The offers come tangled in with the questions. Grain, horses, ships, envoys, promises of mutual defense. Their value depends entirely on who still keeps his word when the next army moves, and I have lately finished learning precisely how many men keep their word with a dragon in the bay.

#bold I will hear every offer. I will bargain from the seat Aegon could not take and my own captains could not sell.#!

ourfury.0202.desc.text:
Reports continue to reach Storm's End from merchants, captains, and men paid to listen in ports where Aegon's ships are known. They agree on very little except that defeat in the stormlands has not ended his ambitions. Good. I would have thought less of him if one bloody nose sent him hiding forever on Dragonstone, though I would sleep better for it.

Whatever lands Aegon now holds, whatever dragons remain to his house, and whatever wars occupy him elsewhere, none of them makes Storm's End safe. He can return himself, send another commander, wait for my death, or whisper terms to lords who resent the price I have made them pay. Only a fool prepares for the enemy he wishes he had, and whatever else my enemies call me, they have not yet proved me a fool.

I will not hold Storm's End forever. Argella will inherit after me, and her heirs after her. What I leave them must be stronger than the circumstances that favored me on one flooded field. Forts, ships, alliances, scouts, and peace where peace can be bought will serve them better than prayers for the same gale. The Seven gave men hands as well as prayers, and I mean to use both. #bold Aegon may come again. Next time I mean for the stormlands to be ready before the clouds gather.#!

ourfury.0202.a.text: Fortify the coast. The next dragon will find us waiting.

ourfury.0202.b.text: Send an envoy. Even Aegon can understand a profitable peace.

ourfury.0202.desc.argella.text:
Reports keep arriving from merchants, captains, and men paid to loiter in ports where Aegon's ships put in. They agree on almost nothing except that one reverse in the stormlands has not ended his ambitions. I would think less of him if it had, though I would sleep a good deal better.

He can come himself. He can send another commander. He can simply wait, which costs him nothing and costs me every year I spend waiting back. Or he can do the cheapest thing available and whisper terms to storm lords who have already discovered what my crown is worth to them under pressure. I know which I would choose in his place.

So the walls go higher, the coast gets watched, the men who held these gates get land, and the men who talked of opening them get remembered. I have no husband and no heirs and a great deal of time in which to acquire both carefully. What I leave behind has to be stronger than one lifted siege and a season of foul weather.

#bold Aegon may come again. Next time I mean for the stormlands to be waiting before the clouds gather.#!

ourfury.0210.desc.text:
The ravens have stopped bringing me bad news, which is a stranger feeling than I expected. Aegon Targaryen came south with three dragons and every kingdom he had already swallowed, and he went home without my crown. Men who spent a year explaining to me why the stormlands could not be held are now explaining to visitors how we held them.

So I have been sitting with a thought I do not much like the look of, and it will not leave. Every argument for why I should have knelt was an argument about dragons. There are fewer dragons now than there were, and the ones that remain have learned to be careful over my country. If the thing that made Aegon inevitable is no longer inevitable, then what exactly is the Trident? What is Highgarden? What is Sunspear?

They are old crowns worn by men who watched the storm break a conqueror and did nothing, because it cost them nothing to wait and see whether I lived. Not one raven of support. Not one spear. They will remember that differently in a year, and so will I.

My lords have not said it aloud, but they have started saying everything that comes just before it. The muster is still standing. The men who beat Orys are still in the field and still fed. There will never be a better moment, and I have never in my life been accused of patience.

#bold I broke the dragon. Now the rest of them can explain why they should not bend the knee to the storm.#!

ourfury.0210.a.text: Draw up the claims. The Trident, the Reach, and Dorne.

ourfury.0210.b.text: The maesters can write it down. I will choose my moment.

fab_ourfury_shattered_shoulder.text: A Shoulder That Will Not Lift

fab_ourfury_undefeated_modifier.text: The King Who Was Not Beaten

fab_conquest_pause.option.text: We need time to prepare before continuing the Conquest.

fab_conquest_pause.tt.text: #I The Conquest will wait upon the King's pleasure. Resume it from the Decisions menu — against whichever kingdom you choose.#!

fab_decision_conquer_riverlands_desc.text: Black Harren sits behind the tallest walls ever raised by man, and the riverlords groan beneath him. Walls are wood and stone, mortar and toil. The towers of Harrenhal are not so tall as Balerion flies — and the Trident waits for a better master.

fab_decision_conquer_riverlands_tooltip.text: Resume the Conquest: take the Riverlands from Harren the Black.

fab_decision_conquer_stormlands_desc.text: Argilac the Arrogant still styles himself the Storm King, and his insult has not been forgotten. Orys shall lead the host south, and Rhaenys shall fly above it. The old man shall have the storm he asked for.

fab_decision_conquer_stormlands_tooltip.text: Resume the Conquest: bring down the last Storm King.

fab_decision_conquer_west.text: Conquer the Reach and the Rock

fab_decision_conquer_west_desc.text: Two kings yet rule beyond the Mander and the Rock — and two kings together are still fewer than three dragons. If Mern and Loren wish to join their hosts against us, we shall oblige them a field to do it on.

fab_decision_conquer_west_tooltip.text: Resume the Conquest: the war for the west — the Reach and the Westerlands both.

fab_decision_conquer_vale.text: Bring the Vale into the Realm

fab_decision_conquer_vale_desc.text: The Falcon perches above the clouds behind her mountains and her Bloody Gate, and thinks herself beyond our reach. Send word to the Eyrie: no pass is high enough to shut out a dragon. We shall hear what terms the Queen Regent offers — or take none.

fab_decision_conquer_vale_tooltip.text: Resume the Conquest: turn upon the Vale of Arryn.

fab_decision_march_on_north_desc.text: South of the Neck the kingdoms are ours; north of it, Torrhen Stark still wears the Crown of Winter. The host will march north through the riverlands to the Neck, with the dragons flying before it — and we shall see whether the King in the North chooses ice or fire.

fab_decision_march_on_north_tooltip.text: Resume the Conquest: march upon the King in the North. The south must be won first.

fab_conquest_north_won.option.text: The North already kneels. The realm grows.

fab_conquest_north_marching.option.text: The host is already marching on the North.

fab_ac_rollback.0001.desc.text: Aegon Targaryen will be remembered not as the founder of a realm, but as the dragonlord whose ambition outran his strength. His defeat leaves House Targaryen with a bitter lesson: dragons inspire terror, yet terror alone cannot guarantee dominion.

fab_ac_rollback.0001.option1.text: A kingdom that will never be.

fab_ac_rollback.0002.desc.text: The attempt to forge one realm from seven has failed. Aegon's name will survive as a warning to later Targaryens that blood and dragons cannot rescue every reckless ambition. Westeros remains divided, and the painted table records a future that never came to pass.

fab_ac_rollback.0002.option1.text: The dream dies with the war.

fab_ac_rollback.0003.desc.loren.text:
The ravens arrive at Casterly Rock in a black procession. Harren Hoare is defeated, his vast river kingdom torn from the ironborn grip. Argilac Durrandon has fallen as well, and the storm crown worn since the days of Durran Godsgrief is no more.

These were not weak kings ruling meager lands. Harren trusted the strongest walls ever built; Argilac had spent a lifetime proving himself in battle. Aegon Targaryen broke them both before the year was out. What began as a foreign lord's impossible boast now advances westward as conquest.

The Rock remains, and Highgarden remains. If lion and green hand are to stop the dragon, we must do what stag and black crown could not: meet fire together, with all the strength of two kingdoms.

fab_ac_rollback.0003.desc.mern.text:
The news is read aloud beneath the green arches of Highgarden. Harren Hoare's river kingdom has been broken and Argilac Durrandon has fallen; two royal lines that ruled before the Andals crossed the narrow sea have been swept aside within a single campaigning season.

Harren believed no fire could master stone. Argilac believed no young conqueror could master him. Their failures leave the lesson plainly written: Aegon must not be allowed to choose the ground, isolate another crown, and bring all three dragons against one kingdom at a time. The Reach has more men than any realm alive, but numbers scattered among castles will burn castle by castle.

Only the Rock can add enough strength to make certainty of advantage. I must bring Loren Lannister into alliance, gather both kingdoms at one field, and force the dragon to face more men than even three beasts can kill.

fab_ac_rollback.0003.desc.text: Harren Hoare and Argilac Durrandon are defeated. The kingdoms of river and storm have fallen before Aegon Targaryen, and two ancient crowns have vanished in a single season.\n\nHarrenhal's walls and Argilac's valor both proved helpless against dragons. What began as an audacious claim from a lord of the narrow sea has become a conquest advancing across Westeros. Every realm still free must now decide whether to stand alone, seek allies, or bend before the fire reaches its borders.

fab_ac_rollback.0003.option.loren.text: Send to Highgarden. The lion will not face the dragon alone.

fab_ac_rollback.0003.option.mern.text: Summon the Reach. Then send my raven to the Rock.

fab_ac_rollback.0003.option1.text: The war has changed. We must prepare.

fab_ac_rollback.0004.text: The Lion and Hand Laid Low

fab_ac_rollback.0004.desc.text: The combined strength of House Lannister and House Gardener has been shattered. The richest kingdoms in Westeros gathered an army without equal, only to see it broken beneath the dragons. \n \nIf Aegon can destroy such a host, every remaining crown must wonder who can still halt him.

fab_ac_rollback.0004.option1.text: The balance of Westeros has broken.

fab_ac_rollback.0005.text: The Crowning of Aegon I Targaryen

fab_ac_rollback.0005.desc.text:
Beneath the crystal dome of Oldtown's Starry Sept, the High Septon anointed Aegon Targaryen with the seven oils and set a crown upon his head. Before the assembled lords and faithful, he proclaimed him #bold Aegon of House Targaryen, the First of His Name, King of the Andals, the Rhoynar, and the First Men, Lord of the Seven Kingdoms, and Protector of the Realm.#!

Visenya had crowned Aegon once already beside the Blackwater, witnessed by only a small company. Here hundreds watched the rite, including the maesters and archmaesters of the Citadel; afterward tens of thousands filled Oldtown's streets as the new king rode Balerion through the city. It is this second crowning that the histories will remember as the beginning of his reign.

With steel, flame, and the strength of his sisters, Aegon has hammered the kingdoms of Westeros into a single realm. Now the Faith itself has blessed what the dragons won.

fab_ac_rollback.0005.option1.text: One realm now stands beneath the dragon's crown.

fab_dorne.0001.desc.text:
Dorne has answered conquest as Dorne answers everything: with sand, stone, and patience.

Thirty thousand spears are said to wait in the Prince's Pass, with near two thousand knights and three hundred lords among them. [fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] leads the royal host down through the red mountains, eager to prove the new rose was planted for more than courtly fragrance. Orys takes a thousand picked knights into the Boneway, where the road narrows and every shadow has a bowstring.

Above them all fly dragons. Rhaenys and Meraxes sweep for the coast, Visenya watches the passes, and I hold the center with Balerion's shadow over my banners.

#bold This is no king's field, nor a wall like Harrenhal. Dorne must be taken by road, well, pass, and thirsting mile.#!

fab_dorne.0002.desc.text:
Rhaenys has made the first mark upon Dorne.

Meraxes came down upon the Planky Town in smoke and terror, and the poleboats of the orphans burned on the Greenblood like festival lanterns. Lemonwood yielded empty halls. Spottswood and Stinkwater opened their gates, and behind those gates my sister found old women, children, and servants who had seen nothing, heard nothing, and could name no man worth burning.

She flew the length of the Greenblood and back again looking for an army. There is none. The shadow city beneath Sunspear stands half deserted, and the old princess herself is nowhere to be found. Wherever the lords of Dorne have gone, they have taken every spear in the country with them and left us their grandmothers.

#bold Dragonfire has found towns, towers, and empty rooms. It has not yet found Dorne.#!

fab_dorne.0003.desc.text:
The deeper we march, the less of Dorne remains before us.

The fields are blackened stubble. The granaries stand open and bare. Wells that should have saved men from the sun stink of rot, poison, and dead things lowered by night. Watchtowers stand abandoned. At one pass our scouts found the road choked by shorn sheep carcasses, piled shoulder-high and ripening in the heat until no horse would come near it.

No banner has offered battle, and no lord has come out to defend the stones that bear his name. The Dornish make themselves felt in every arrow from the rocks, every shuttered window, every empty road where our host eats dust and sees no enemy worth charging.

#bold Harren hid behind stone. The Dornish have made a fortress of absence, heat, and sand.#!

fab_dorne.0003.option1.text: This war will be thirsty work.

fab_dorne.0004.desc.text:
A single road will not win this war.

Every castle we take stands empty. Every valley swallows outriders whole. Every raven I send south comes back carrying nothing but my own questions. Dorne cannot be brought to battle on one front for the simplest of reasons: Dorne does not mean to be brought to battle at all.

So the host divides. [fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] turns the strength of the Reach toward the Hellholt, where the Ullers are said to keep their scorpions and their knives in equal number. I take the eastern road for Skyreach and the Fowler passes. Orys presses on up the Boneway, hard as ever, unwilling to let red stone and cowards' arrows halt the king's right hand.

If Dorne will not stand in one place to be conquered, we shall take it in pieces.

#bold Somewhere in these sands sits the blind old woman who chose this war. One of my hosts will find her.#!

fab_dorne.0004.option1.text: Divide the host. Take the castles.

fab_dorne.0005.desc.text:
[fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] has reached the Hellholt with a host no singer will envy.

A quarter of the men are gone to thirst, fever, broken feet, and arrows loosed from places no outrider could reach in time. Nearly all the horses are dead. Every waterhole was fouled; every oasis had been poisoned before the van came within sight of it. Men who wore green at Highgarden now stagger beneath brown cloaks stiff with salt and dust.

The Hellholt gave the Reach walls, sun, and silence. Its halls were empty by the time the Tyrell banners appeared, and [fab_reach_lord.GetSheHe] was left to count the dead before a castle that had refused even the dignity of surrender.

#bold A dragon may fly over the desert. An army must cross it.#!

fab_dorne.0005.option1.text: The desert bleeds us without showing a blade.

fab_dorne.0006.desc.text:
Skyreach is ours, after a fashion. Some men swear we stormed it; others say the gates stood open before the first ladder touched stone. In Dorne both tales can be true, and men die taking empty castles all the same.

Yronwood held longer, though not with the strength its name once promised. Old men, boys, and women watched from the walls, and when the fighting was done and we counted the fallen, there was scarcely a man of fighting age among them. The Tor was handed over by its steward - Lord Jordayne lately dead, and no heir minded to die for stones his own princess had already written off.

I garrison what I take. I set banners on the towers and castellans in the halls, and every night the sentries watch roads down which no one ever comes. The castles are mine. Dorne is somewhere else.

#bold We are winning castles from ghosts.#!

fab_dorne.0006.option1.text: Garrison them all. Dorne must be somewhere.

fab_dorne.0007.desc.text:
At Ghost Hill, House Toland sends forth a champion beneath bright arms and brighter insolence. He names himself the sword of his lord, the shield of his house, the wrath of Dorne in one man's body, and dares the dragon to meet him on the ground.

Behind him, the castle watches. My own captains mutter that no king need answer such theater. Their caution has merit, yet Blackfyre hangs at my hip, and every Dornish eye in the hills is waiting to see whether Aegon Targaryen needs a dragon to kill one boastful man.

#bold The singers will have their duel, then.#!

fab_dorne.0007.option1.text: Come then. Let us see this champion.

fab_dorne.0008.desc.text:
The raven from the Boneway is written by a shaking hand.

Orys marched where the mountains pinch the road to a wound. Rocks came down first, then arrows, then spears from above. Men who survived the daylight were murdered in the dark. By morning the path was blocked before and behind, and the Dornish came from every ledge where no army should have been able to stand.

A thousand knights entered the Boneway. Most are dead. A dozen lords are taken. If the survivors speak true, Orys himself has vanished into the hands of the Wyl of Wyl.

The man who was my shield and strong right hand is now somewhere in the red mountains, beyond ransom, threat, or dragonfire.

#bold Dorne has drawn blood from the crown.#!

fab_dorne.0008.option1.text: Find where they have taken him.

fab_dorne.0009.desc.text:
At Sunspear, beneath painted spears and the old banners of Nymeria's line, Dorne has been declared taken.

The halls were full for the ceremony: crownlanders, reachmen, stormlanders, captains of the host, and such Dornish dignitaries as could be found or compelled to stand witness. The Martell sun was lowered. The dragon was raised. [fab_sunspear_castellan.GetTitledFirstName] is named castellan of Sunspear and Warden of the Sands, charged to hold what dragons and spears have won.

Men cheered because men must cheer when a king has crossed a desert and calls it victory.

The shadow city watched from shuttered windows, and beyond the walls the sands kept very quiet.

#bold Dorne is mine. Now it must learn to stay mine.#!

fab_dorne.0010.desc.text:
I have come home through the Prince's Pass, and the realm calls Dorne conquered.

[fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] remains at the Hellholt with what is left of [fab_reach_lord.GetHerHis] host, and the letters grow shorter each time. The men sicken on fish drawn from the sulfurous Brimstone and curse every cup before they dare to drink it. Patrols sent toward Sandstone and Vaith do not come back beaten - they do not come back at all, horses and mail and men together. Qorgyle riders strike out of the noon glare and are gone before any pursuit can even form.

In the capital they toast seven kingdoms under one throne, and the singers are already quarreling over who gets to have crossed the desert first. In Dorne, men keep dying on roads we have already won. I have left [fab_sunspear_castellan.GetTitledFirstName] a palace, [fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] a furnace, and both of them my luck.

#bold The map is cleaner than the war.#!

fab_dorne.0010.option1.text: [fab_sunspear_castellan.GetTitledFirstName] will hold Sunspear, and [fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] the marches.

fab_dorne.0011.desc.text:
Dorne has risen behind us like fire under ash.

Skyreach, Yronwood, the Tor, and Ghost Hill have all been retaken, their garrisons put to the sword. Castellans are dragged from halls and towers, tortured, broken, and displayed for every Dornish child to remember. The shadow city has poured back into Sunspear with knives under cloaks and stones in every hand.

[fab_sunspear_castellan.GetTitledFirstName], my Warden of the Sands, was hauled through the Spear Tower by men who had bowed to him only days before. They brought him before Meria Martell in the high chamber, where the old princess sat beneath the sun-and-spear with blind eyes turned toward his voice. He begged to be ransomed. Meria asked whether Aegon had ransomed the dead left in the Prince's Pass.

At her command, the windows were opened. My castellan was dragged across the tiles, lifted struggling onto the sill, and thrown out over the city he had been named to rule. The crowd below cheered when he struck the stones.

By dusk the Martell sun flew over Sunspear again, and every Dornish throat in the shadow city knew the sound of freedom.

#bold We conquered an empty land. The Dornish waited until we had to hold it.#!

fab_dorne.0012.desc.text:
[fab_reach_lord.GetTitledFirstName] marched from the Hellholt for Vaith and Sunspear, and no certain word has followed the host north.

Scouts found dead horses first, then broken spears, then a cookfire cold beneath a cliff where no army had any cause to camp. The desert gives back scraps when it wishes to be cruel. It has not given back the lord of Highgarden, nor the host that followed [fab_reach_lord.GetHerHim] into the sands.

Highgarden will have a new lord, and the Reach will have a wound that no raven can explain. Dorne has swallowed a Lord Paramount whole.

#bold Some castles can be taken. Some deserts only take.#!

fab_dorne.0012.option1.text: The rose has vanished in the sand.

fab_dorne.0013.desc.text:
The council demands an answer.

Visenya would burn every road from the Prince's Pass to the Greenblood. The stormlords rage for Orys and the hands Dorne may yet take from him. The reachmen look south with fear and shame in equal measure, wondering how many more green sons the sands will swallow before the Martells admit they are beaten.

Dorne has forced a harder question than any siege: what does beaten mean when castles fall and rise again, when lords vanish and still command, when an old princess can throw my castellan from a tower while my banners are scarcely home?

I can loose fire and blood until the deserts glow red, or I can let the old woman keep her sands and name the war finished before it takes more than pride.

#bold Dorne remains unconquered. The choice is whether I can endure that.#!

fab_dorne.0013.option1.text: No. Fire and blood, until Dorne remembers.

fab_dorne.0013.option3.text: Not now. But Dorne's day will come.

fab_dorne.0015.desc.text:
Blackfyre answers the jest quickly enough. The champion comes on in bright steel and falls in the dust before his challenge has fully left the air. It was no great stroke that killed him. He fought like a man who had never held a sword outside a mummer's show - and, as it happens, he had not.

The laughter behind Toland's walls begins only after he falls. The man was no knight. He was Lord Toland's fool, dressed in his lord's own armor and sent out to caper and die while the household slipped away behind the hill.

By the time our men force the gates, Ghost Hill is empty - soldiers, stores, and banners gone, the larders swept bare, not a Toland left to hang. All that remains is a dead jester in borrowed steel and the sound of Dornish laughter carrying a long way over stone.

#bold They spend fools like knights and call it victory. Some days I could almost believe it is one.#!

fab_dorne.0017.desc.text:
The second war has little use for banners.

There will be no fields won in this one, no thrones taken, no morning where two hosts stand across a valley and settle the matter like the Field of Fire. Dornish riders strike the baggage trains and vanish into ravines that were not on any map. Wells are filled with carrion. My messengers are found hanging from dry trees with the royal seals still tied to their wrists. Castles kneel by day and open their postern gates by night, and the same lord who swears me fealty at noon sends my patrol routes south by dusk.

It will be raids and reprisals, murders and little truces made to be broken - a long red grinding of knives, with a dozen small peaces in it and no peace at all.

Visenya says fear must be made larger than the desert. I answer her with dragons, with hangings, and with gold for every man who will sell us a name.

#bold Dorne has chosen knives. We will answer with fire.#!

fab_dorne.0017.option1.text: Then they will learn what fire costs.

fab_dorne.0018.desc.text:
The ransom wagons came south under guard, their wheels sunk deep with gold.

The Wyls had named their price without shame: Lord Orys Baratheon's weight in gold, and the weight of every stormlander taken with him. Coin by coin, bar by bar, the ransom was counted before Dornish witnesses. I would leave no stormlord to rot for want of payment, and I would give no man cause to say the Iron Throne had abandoned its own.

Once the gold belonged to them, the Wyls opened the prison doors.

Orys came out pale, thinner, and silent. Behind him came his bannermen, each man staring at the bandaged ruin where his sword hand had been. The Dornish had taken the ransom and then taken the hands as well, so none of them would ever raise steel against Dorne again.

When Orys knelt, he did it slowly. Blood had soaked through the linen at his wrist. He would not look at it. He looked at me instead, and the hall went quiet enough to hear the flies at the bandages.

#bold Dorne has sold me my brother back by weight, and kept the part of him that held a sword.#!

fab_dorne.0019.desc.text:
The Boneway glowed red beneath Balerion.

House Wyl's mountain fastnesses clung to the stone like claws: towers above the pass, halls cut into the rock, goat tracks, murder holes, and black cave mouths where whole households could vanish. Balerion answered all of it with fire.

The outer walls cracked first. The gates sagged and ran with molten iron. Roofs burst inward. Storehouses, kennels, stables, rope bridges, watchtowers, painted shields, and the little sept under the cliff burned until smoke rolled through the pass like a second night.

The Wyls knew their own mountain too well to die in the halls above. They fled downward into caves and tunnels while the castle became rubble over their heads. Men dragged from the yards screamed their lord's name and died without telling where he had gone.

By dusk, no fastness stood above ground. Hot stone, dead horses, and blackened banners snapped in Balerion's wind.

#bold I burned Wyl to rubble. Dorne hid beneath the rubble and lived.#!

fab_dorne.0020.desc.text:
The war has crossed its own borders.

A Dornish captain who styles himself a pirate king of the Stepstones has fallen upon Cape Wrath with raiders and sellsails, sacking half a dozen towns beneath the stormlords' noses - and behind him the rainwood itself is burning. Fowler men came over the mountains by night and took Nightsong, carrying the Carons off to Dorne as hostages and leaving the castle in smoke. Farther west, Joffrey Dayne rode to the very gates of Oldtown and put the torch to every field, mill, and village in sight of the Hightower. Ser Garmon Hightower led the knights out against him and was slain; his kin retook nothing but ashes and stubble.

Visenya has already carried the answer south - Lemonwood, Ghost Hill, and the Tor burned in a single turn of the moon. And still the raids come. A conquest map cannot hold this shape. Dorne bleeds outward like poison in water.

#bold They cannot beat dragons in the sky, so they make every shore and every road a wound.#!

fab_dorne.0021.desc.text:
The raven from the south carries the worst word of the war.

Rhaenys went to the Hellholt as I bade her, and she went as she has always gone - low and unhurried, out of a clean sky, certain that nothing below could reach her. Nothing ever had.

Something reached her. A scorpion mounted on the highest tower held its shot until the silver queen filled the sky above it, and the iron bolt took Meraxes through the eye.

The dragon screamed so that men on the walls dropped their spears and fell to their knees with their hands over their ears. Her wings beat once, twice, and failed. Meraxes came down upon the Hellholt like the wrath of every god at once, taking the tower that killed her and half the curtain wall into ruin beneath her, and the fires she had set became the fires that buried her.

#bold And after, the sky over the Hellholt stayed empty.#!

fab_dorne.0022.desc.text:
We were children in this hall, the three of us.

Rhaenys used to dance along that gallery while the septa scolded her hoarse. She sang sailors' songs at supper - the ones with the verses no queen should know - until even Visenya laughed against her will. There is no stone in this castle that does not have her voice somewhere inside it. I keep catching myself listening for her step on the stair. Then I remember. The remembering is a blade drawn fresh every time.

There is no body. That is the part I cannot carry. Nothing to burn, nothing to lay in the sept, no ashes to give the wind. Only silence out of the south - and under the silence, the whispers I have forbidden and cannot stop hearing. That she did not die when Meraxes fell. That the Ullers pulled her from the wreck. That somewhere beneath Dornish stone my little sister lived on in the dark, and called for us, and we did not come.

Visenya has not wept where any man could see her. Tonight, in this cold hall, she weeps - standing straight as a spear, eyes open, as if grief were one more enemy she will not kneel to. I look at the Painted Table, at the little carved mountains of Dorne our forefathers made, and my face is wet before I know it.

She was the best of us. The kindest. The one people loved without being taught to. Now Dorne will learn what her brother and sister are without her.

#bold Grief has its hour. Then the dragons have theirs.#!

fab_dorne.0022.option1.text: Fire and blood, until the sands remember her.

fab_dorne.0023.desc.text:
Gold rides south faster than armies.

I have set a price on Dorne. A lord's weight in gold for Fowler. A castle's ransom for Vaith and for Toland. And for Uller of the Hellholt, beneath whose walls my sister fell, enough to buy a fleet. The ravens carry my promises into every court, tavern, and counting house from the Wall to the Free Cities. Some men kill for loyalty. Far more will kill for what I am offering.

The sands have begun to pay already. Four Lords Uller have died in the Hellholt since the bounty was first cried - one after another, by knife and fall and poisoned cup - though of the men who did the work, only two lived long enough to collect.

And Dorne, being Dorne, has opened a purse of its own. Lord Connington took an arrow through the throat while hunting his own woods. Lord Mertyns' entire household died at table of poisoned wine. Lord Fell was found smothered in a King's Landing brothel. This war has no battlefields left. It has prices.

#bold Every shadow in Dorne will wonder what it is worth. Mine already do.#!

fab_dorne.0024.desc.text:
The singers were still at the first refrain when the doors were barred.

Cafferen and Oakheart blood had met beneath garlands and candlelight. Children chased one another under the benches. The bridegroom stood to drink, smiling, and that was when the Wyl men showed themselves. Crossbows came down from the gallery. Knives came out beneath serving cloths. The hall filled with screaming so quickly the music did not have time to stop.

Lords died with cups in their hands. Knights were cut down unarmed. The bridegroom was gelded before his own guests and left to choke on wine and blood. The bride and her women were dragged from the feast while the tables burned behind them.

By morning the wedding hall was quiet, save for flies.

#bold There are crimes even war should be ashamed to claim.#!

fab_dorne.0025.desc.text:
Meria Martell is dead.

Fire did not take her from the saddle, nor did gold buy a knife close enough to end her. The old princess died in her bed with blind eyes closed, her sands still unconquered and her people still calling her unconquered too. After all my hosts, vows, and dragonfire, she has taken the ending she chose.

Her son Nymor takes up the rule of Dorne: old, cautious, and surrounded by a country blasted from the Red Mountains to the mouth of the Greenblood. Still the Dornish fight.

#bold Even death has not delivered me the victory Meria denied.#!

fab_dorne.0025.option1.text: The son will answer for it.

fab_dorne.0026.desc.text:
Deria Martell has come to King's Landing.

Nymor sends his daughter with an escort, a peace envoy in silk and sun colors, and before her men carry the skull of Meraxes. White bone. Blackened ruin. The empty socket where the scorpion bolt went in. The court mutters murder.

Orys stands among the stormlords, sleeve pinned where his sword hand used to be. "Send her back to her father without a hand," he says, not loudly, not wildly, but with the cold certainty of a man who has paid for mercy and learned its Dornish price.

Visenya looks as though she might kill the girl where she kneels.

Deria does not flinch. She offers peace without submission, and a sealed letter from her father.

For a moment all I can see is the hollow where Meraxes's eye once burned.

#bold Dorne has brought my dead into my hall, and every living wound demands an answer.#!

fab_dorne.0027.desc.text:
The court is waiting when I return.

Deria Martell stands beneath the Iron Throne with Meraxes's skull behind her and all the realm's fury pointed at her throat. Visenya says nothing. Orys says too much with one empty sleeve. The stormlords remember their maimed kin. The crownlords remember Rhaenys. Every man in the hall expects fire, imprisonment, or some final payment for the long years of defiance.

I give them peace.

Deria leaves King's Landing with both hands. The embassy suffers no reprisal, no dragon flies south, and no bounty is paid for Martell blood. Dorne will remain outside my realm, unbowed and unbroken, and the treaty will bear my seal before the sun is high.

After I refuse the first question, the court learns to leave Nymor's letter unnamed.

#bold The realm remains six kingdoms and a wound.#!

fab_dorne.0028.desc.text:
Every account of Rhaenys's end contradicts the last.

Some swear she lost her seat in the fall and struck the stones before Meraxes shattered the yard. Others claim the dragon crushed her beneath broken wing and burning scale. A few uglier reports say she lived after the fall, that Uller men found her in the wreckage and kept her breathing in torment while the castle burned around them.

Neither truth nor body has come north. Silence has crossed the sands in their place, broad enough to carry every rumor and cruel enough to make each one possible.

#bold Dorne has killed a dragon and taken a queen.#!

fab_dorne.0028.option1.text: End this war and bring me fire.

fab_dorne.0029.desc.text:
Balerion's shadow crossed the chosen Dornish seat before the sun reached noon.

The castle below had barred its gates and hidden its banners, as though wood and silence could make stone innocent. I gave no summons. Rhaenys had been given none at Hellholt. Black wings blotted out the yard, the towers, the wells, and the little sept where servants fled to pray. The Black Dread opened his mouth, and the stones learned what a dragon's grief sounds like.

When the fire passed, the roofs were gone. Men crawled from cellars with their hair smoking. Ravens rose black against black smoke, then fell again when the heat took them.

#bold One stronghold burned. Dorne has many.#!

fab_dorne.0030.desc.text:
Visenya returned with soot on her armor and no softness in her face.

She said the lord watched from his own walls until Vhagar folded her wings and fell upon the castle like judgment. Scorpions burned before they loosed. The gatehouse split. Every granary went up in such bright fire that riders saw it from three valleys away.

The Dornish may rebuild; stubbornness has always been cheaper than submission. When the stones rise again, Vhagar can teach them the same lesson with less patience.

#bold Once is warning. Twice is memory. Thrice is law.#!

fab_dorne.0030.option1.text: Visenya will choose the next road.

fab_dorne.0031.text: The Dragon's Wroth: No Safe Walls

fab_dorne.0031.desc.text:
The latest Dornish lord had emptied the halls before we arrived.

He can hear the story from those who ran. Balerion burned the seat anyway: the stables, the armory, the carved doors, the painted shields, the nursery windows, and the rookery where frightened birds beat themselves bloody against their cages. Fire does not need a lord present to make a lord poorer.

By dusk the castle was a red shell, and every village for miles could smell hot lime, cooked grain, and old pride turning to smoke.

#bold Dorne hides its lords. It cannot hide their homes.#!

fab_dorne.0032.desc.text:
I read the letter upon the Iron Throne.

The maesters record none of the words, and the lords below the steps stand too far away to see the hand. Men will say later that my fist closed too tightly on the blades, and that when I rose, my palm was dripping blood onto the steps.

Nymor may have written as one father to another. He may have named every dead lord, knight, child, and queen the war has swallowed. He may have claimed Rhaenys lived after Hellholt, with Dorne holding the power to end her torment. He may have promised to spend every coin in the sands on knives from Braavos and named my son as their price.

The letter burns before anyone can ask to read it, and the smoke carries away the only certain truth in the hall.

#bold Some words are sharper than dragonbone.#!

fab_dorne.0033.desc.text:
Balerion climbs into the dark with King's Landing shrinking beneath us.

The letter is ash. My hand still bleeds. The wind takes the smoke from my cloak and tears it away over Blackwater Bay. Dragonstone rises ahead from the sea, black and familiar, the old heart of my house. I go there without court, council, or singers to make the choice noble after the fact.

Stone, night, and Nymor's question wait for me there. By dawn, the realm will have an answer.

#bold The dragon flies north, and Dorne lives another night.#!

fab_dorne.0035.desc.text:
Orys came to council with his right sleeve pinned across his chest.

The court tried to leave the wound unnamed, and the silence made a spectacle of him. Lords who had laughed with him at feasts stared into their cups. Petitioners lowered their eyes. The chair beside mine, the chair of the Hand, seemed built for a different man: the stormlord who had broken Argilac beneath black rain, who had ridden hard roads for me, who had made my commands into war.

Orys stood before it for a long moment and then pushed the chair back.

"The King's Hand should have a hand," he said. His voice was flat as old iron. "I will not have men speaking of the King's Stump."

He would return to the stormlands with Wyl written into him more deeply than any scar. Healing was the word the maesters used; vengeance was the word Orys carried home.

#bold My first Hand leaves me with one hand less in the realm, and one more oath of vengeance.#!

fab_dorne.0036.desc.text:
The Aegonfort is a warren of raw timber and torchlight, and I have walked its passages a thousand nights without thinking of them once.

Tonight a man in the livery of my own kitchens is waiting where the corridor turns toward my chambers. The candles have been snuffed. I hear him before I see him, and I see the knife last of all.

He never reaches me. A guardsman - I do not know his name, and I am ashamed of that - puts his shoulder between us and takes the blade along his ribs, and the second guard opens the man's throat against the wall. It is over before I have drawn breath to shout.

They strip the body and find sand in his boot heels and a purse of Dornish gold sewn into his shirt. I set a price on the lords of Dorne, and Dorne has answered in kind. The difference is that they need only be fortunate once.

The guardsman who bled for me will have lands, a knighthood, whatever he asks. The dead man will have a hole in the ground. And I will have new locks, new tasters, and a longer walk to my bed.

fab_dorne.0036.option1.text: Double the watch. Reward that man.

fab_dorne.0037.desc.text:
Four moons of doubled guards, and it has made me careless in the one place no king thinks to be watchful: his own stable yard, at dawn, among servants he sees every day.

The groom holding the feeding cart is not my groom. I know it the way a swordsman knows things, in the hands and not the head - he moves wrong, he watches wrong, and when I turn he is already inside the reach of any shout for help, a curved Dornish knife sliding out of his sleeve.

But I have carried Blackfyre every waking hour since the night in the corridor. Visenya asked that much of me, and I am done arguing with her.

Valyrian steel is out of the scabbard before his knife clears the sleeve. He is quick. The blade is quicker. I leave him in the straw and stand alone in the grey light, breathing hard, listening to the guards come running - too late, again - and I think for the first time that my sister may be right about more than the sword.

Twice now. The third knife is already on the road. Every man in this castle knows it, and so do I.

fab_dorne.0037.option1.text: I killed him myself. This time.

fab_dorne.0038.desc.text:
A king who hides in his fort is no king, so I ride down into the city that has grown around it - and Visenya rides with me, in silk over mail, as she always is now.

It happens among the fish stalls and the cordwainers' benches, where the crowd presses closest. Two men come out of the press of petitioners with the dust of the road still on them. The first dies with his dagger half-raised, opened wrist to elbow before my guards have so much as turned their heads. The second actually touches my bridle. He is reaching up when Dark Sister goes through him, once, and Visenya is somehow past me and back again, and both men are bleeding into the mud between one heartbeat and the next.

My guards arrive after. They always arrive after.

My sister looks at them the way she looks at a broken sword, then at me, and she does not say a word. She does not have to. Three knives in a year, and the only blade that has ever mattered was hers.

We ride back to the Aegonfort in silence. I know my sister. This silence is her drawing breath.

fab_dorne.0038.option1.text: Say it, sister. You will anyway.

fab_dorne.0039.desc.text:
She comes to me in the hall when the court is thin, wearing mail beneath her silks - night and day she wears it now - and asks me one more time to do the same.

I tell her no. I tell her what I have told her since the stable yard: #bold 'I have my guards.'#!

I do not see her move. That is the whole of it - I, who broke two kings on one field, do not see my own sister move. There is a line of cold across my cheek, Dark Sister is already sliding home in its scabbard, my guardsmen are only now reaching for their hilts, and my blood is on the queen's blade.

#bold 'Your guards are slow and lazy,'#! Visenya says. #bold 'I could have killed you as easily as I cut you. Even with Blackfyre in your hand, you are only one man - and I cannot always be with you.'#!

The guards stand frozen, waiting to see if their king will call this treason. I put my fingers to my cheek and they come away red, and what I feel is not anger at all.

She is right. Gods help me, she has been right since the first knife.

fab_dorne.0039.option1.text: You have made your point, sister.

fab_dorne.0040.desc.text:
The cut on my cheek has scabbed by the time Visenya lays her design before me, and it is a design - she has thought it through as thoroughly as she ever thought through a war.

Kings have always kept champions. I am lord of the Seven Kingdoms, she says, and so I shall have seven: the finest knights in the realm, sworn not to a castle or a wage but to my life, men who sleep across my door and go where I go. She would have their vows cut from the same cloth as the Night's Watch oath. They will serve for life. They will hold no lands, take no wives, father no children, claim no glory but the guarding of the king. White cloaks, white shields, white scale - so that all men may know them at a glance, and so that they may never be mistaken for anything but what they are.

I tell her we shall hold a great tourney to find them, and for a moment I am pleased with myself. Visenya is not. A tourney finds the swiftest sword, she says, and a swift sword can be bought - it was not skill we lacked in the fish market. What the seven must have cannot be judged from a gallery: it is loyalty. She will choose them herself, one by one, and she will look each man in the eye as she does it.

I have trusted her judgment on greater things. I trust it on this.

fab_dorne.0040.option1.text: Then choose them, sister. Choose well.

fab_dorne.0041.desc.text:
Seven knights kneel on the boards below the Iron Throne, and the steam of their breath rises in the cold of the hall.

Ser Richard Roote. Ser Addison Hill, the Bastard of Cornfield. Ser Gregor Goode and Ser Griffith Goode, blood of one house. Ser Humfrey, whom the smallfolk call the Mummer. Ser Robin Darklyn, that men name Darkrobin, first of the old blood of Duskendale to take the cloak. And at their head Ser Corlys Velaryon of Driftmark, my own kin by the salt of the old blood, who shall be the first to command them.

One by one they say the words my sister wrote for them. They give up their lands and their claims, the wives they will never take and the sons they will never father, their places at every table but mine. They will win no glory and hold no halls. They serve for life, and the life they guard is mine.

The cloaks go over their shoulders white as new snow, and the hall is very quiet. Even Visenya, who chose every man of them and trusts nothing in this world she cannot hold, watches with something close to satisfaction.

Seven kingdoms. Seven gods. Seven swords between the king and every knife in the dark. Dorne may send what it will.

fab_dorne.0041.option1.text: Rise, Ser Corlys. Guard your king.

fab_dorne.0043.desc.aenys.text:
Dragonstone takes me in without a word, the way old houses take back their children.

As for what Nymor wrote to me - the words are ash over Blackwater Bay, and ash they will remain. The maesters may guess. The singers may lie. Visenya herself may ask me with her hand on Dark Sister, and it will change nothing. Some things a king carries alone, and this one I will carry to my grave.

I mean to sit the night with the Painted Table, and instead my feet carry me to the nursery door. [fab_rhaenys_child.GetFirstName] is asleep with [fab_rhaenys_child.GetHerHis] silver hair across the pillow, small beneath the blankets, and the young dragon that hatched in [fab_rhaenys_child.GetHerHis] cradle lies curled at the foot of the bed like a cat made of pale flame. Rhaenys carried [fab_rhaenys_child.GetHerHim] in this castle while the realm made war. So few years she had of [fab_rhaenys_child.GetHerHim]. She saw the first steps taken on these very stones - and she will never see the rest of it, the first flight, the first vows, the day the child's face becomes one she would have known anywhere, and [fab_rhaenys_child.GetFirstName] will remember her as a warmth more than a face.

When I turn from the bed she is there - by the window where she always stood, where the salt wind used to catch her hair. Grief, the maesters would say, and no ghost. On Dragonstone the difference has always been thin. She does not speak. She looks at our sleeping child, and then at me, and her eyes ask the only question left in the world.

#bold By dawn I must answer her, and Nymor, and the child behind me.#!

fab_dorne.0043.desc.nochild.text:
Dragonstone takes me in without a word, the way old houses take back their children.

As for what Nymor wrote to me - the words are ash over Blackwater Bay, and ash they will remain. The maesters may guess. The singers may lie. Visenya herself may ask me with her hand on Dark Sister, and it will change nothing. Some things a king carries alone, and this one I will carry to my grave.

I mean to sit the night with the Painted Table, and instead my feet carry me to a door I ordered built and never speak of: the nursery. It is swept and cold. No cradle was ever warmed in it. Rhaenys wanted children the way she wanted the sky - laughing, certain, in no hurry at all, as though the years belonged to us. A boy with her eyes, she said once, and her seat on a dragon, and none of my brooding. We had a war first, we told ourselves. There was time.

When I turn from the empty room she is there - by the window where she always stood, where the salt wind used to catch her hair. Grief, the maesters would say, and no ghost. On Dragonstone the difference has always been thin. She does not speak. She looks at the room that never held our child, and then at me, and her eyes ask the only question left in the world.

#bold By dawn I must answer her, and Nymor, and the empty room behind me.#!

fab_dorne.0043.option1.text: At dawn. At dawn I will answer.

fab_dorne.0048.desc.text:
A year has passed since the realm was proclaimed whole, and the proclamation still has a hole in it the shape of Dorne.

Six kingdoms answer to the Iron Throne in more than name. The seventh sits behind its mountains and its sands as though the Conquest were a rumor from across the sea. The council will not let the matter rest. Visenya names every moon Dorne stands apart a lesson to any lord who dreams of standing apart likewise. The marcher lords ask whose peace runs in the Prince's Pass and the Boneway, and get no answer worth the raven. Merchants pay Martell tolls on the Greenblood and wonder aloud, in my own hall, whether the old woman in Sunspear frightened the dragons after all.

Meria Martell was warned that I would return with fire and blood. A king's warnings do not age well unspent - yet Dorne has broken no peace, and deserts drink armies as readily as they drink rain.

#bold One kingdom remains outside my realm. The question is put to me plainly: now, later, or never?#!

fab_dorne.0048.option1.text: Now. Fire and Blood, as Meria was promised.

fab_dorne.0048.option2.text: Not yet. Dorne will keep - and the choice stays mine.

fab_dorne.0049.desc.text:
The war has finally tilted.

What spears Dorne has left are penned up behind whatever walls the dragons have spared them, and the proudest of those walls is the Hellholt - the Ullers' seat on the Brimstone, a byword for treachery even among Dornishmen. Every lord still refusing me looks to it. While it stands, no knee in Dorne has to be the first to bend.

Rhaenys wants it. Nothing in Dorne has yet come close to touching Meraxes, she reminds me; one pass over the towers and the Ullers will be on their knees before their granaries catch. My captains talk instead of siege lines on the Brimstone, of sappers and hunger and patience. Months, in that furnace of a valley. And men - the desert has never been cheap with my men.

#bold The Hellholt must submit. What remains is to decide what I will spend on it.#!

fab_dorne.0049.option1.text: We will send Queen Rhaenys with Meraxes to ensure their submission.

fab_dorne.0049.option2.text: We will take the Hellholt by conventional means - siege lines and patience.

fab_dorne.0050.desc.text:
The great doors stand open, and the sun-and-spear of House Martell is carried the length of my hall - lowered.

There was no single day this war was won. The Hellholt starved until even Uller pride ran dry. The passes were taken a thirsting mile at a time, garrisoned, and this once never given back. Castle by castle the sands ran out of places to hide an army, and Dorne - never beaten in the field - woke one morning to find there was no field left.

Now [fab_dorne_kneeler.GetTitledFirstName] kneels below the Iron Throne, before the lords of six kingdoms that today become seven. [fab_dorne_kneeler.GetSheHe|U] does not speak the old boast of Sunspear, and no one in the hall speaks it for [fab_dorne_kneeler.GetHerHim]. Unbowed, unbent, unbroken - there is no need to say it. Every eye can see how the boast ends.

Bowed. Bent. And unbroken only because I will it so: Dorne keeps its lords, [fab_dorne_kneeler.GetFirstName] keeps the sun-and-spear, and all of it passes beneath the dragon's wing.

#bold Seven kingdoms. One realm. Ring the bells.#!

fab_dorne.0051.desc.text:
Dorne knelt. Not every Dornishman was in the hall.

Tonight a man in kitchen livery waited where the corridor turns toward my chambers, in the dark of candles someone had snuffed for him. If the guardsman at my shoulder had been a step slower, the histories would say Aegon survived the war with Dorne and died of the peace. The guardsman took the knife along his ribs instead, and the second guard opened the man's throat against the wall before I had drawn breath to shout.

There was sand in the dead man's boot heels. Knotted at his wrist was a strip of orange silk - the sun-and-spear, torn into a mourning band. No lord sent him; the lords made their peace and mean to keep it. But a defeated country is full of men nobody consulted, and every one of them knows my face.

#bold Dorne bowed. Some of its knives have not heard.#!

fab_dorne.0051.option1.text: Reward that man. And find me the rest of them.

fab_dorne.0052.desc.text:
Visenya finds me when the court is thin. She does not ask this time. She tells me.

I have won Dorne, she says, and in winning it I have salted my own realm with its angriest sons - men with no war left and nothing to lose. A kingdom taken by patience must be kept by vigilance, and my guards, she observes, possess neither.

I tell her I have my guards. I do not see her move. There is a line of cold across my cheek, Dark Sister is already sliding home, and my blood is on the queen's blade while my guardsmen are still reaching for their hilts.

#bold 'You conquered Dorne without losing so much as a dragon,'#! she says. #bold 'It would be a poor jest to lose the king to a kitchen knife. Seven kingdoms, brother. Seven swords, sworn for life - and I will choose every one of them myself.'#!

She is right. She has been right since the corridor.

fab_dorne.0052.option1.text: Then choose them, sister. Choose well.

fab_dorne.0053.desc.text:
Seven knights kneel on the boards below the Iron Throne, and the steam of their breath rises in the cold of the hall.

Ser Richard Roote. Ser Addison Hill, the Bastard of Cornfield. Ser Gregor Goode and Ser Griffith Goode, blood of one house. Ser Humfrey, whom the smallfolk call the Mummer. Ser Robin Darklyn, that men name Darkrobin. And at their head Ser Corlys Velaryon of Driftmark, my own kin by the salt of the old blood, first to command them.
