Some swear my mother woke and consented; others swear she never woke at all. I know only that she died giving birth to a daughter, Jocelyn.\n\n#bold The storm has taken the gentlest soul it ever held.#!

sotd_lifeline.0003.a.text: She woke, and consented. I must believe that.

sotd_lifeline.0003.b.text: She never woke. Perhaps that was the gods' one mercy.

nick_sotd_the_boy_king_desc.text: Crowned in the Starry Sept at four-and-ten, with his mother ruling as Queen Regent and Lord Rogar Baratheon as Protector of the Realm, [CHARACTER.GetShortUINameNoTooltipNoFormat] is known throughout the Seven Kingdoms as 'the Boy King' - a name [CharYouSheHe(CHARACTER)] means to outgrow.

nick_sotd_the_justified_desc.text: After the Trial of Seven was won, the king became known as Jaehaerys the Justified, for in the sight of gods and men alike his cause had prevailed.

nick_sotd_the_forsaken_desc.text: The gods themselves were asked to judge [CHARACTER.GetShortUINameNoTooltipNoFormat] in a Trial of Seven, and the gods judged against [CharYouHerHim(CHARACTER)]. Abandoned by the Seven and stripped of all [CharYouSheHe(CHARACTER)] loved, [CharYouSheHe(CHARACTER)] [CharAreIs(CHARACTER)] known as 'the Forsaken.'

nick_sotd_the_cruel_desc.text: [CHARACTER.GetShortUINameNoTooltipNoFormat] loosed dragonfire upon the Starry Sept, the holiest house of the Seven, and burned the High Septon alive within it. Like [CharYourHerHis(CHARACTER)] uncle Maegor before [CharYouHerHim(CHARACTER)], the realm shall remember [CharYouHerHim(CHARACTER)] as 'the Cruel.'

nick_sotd_the_brave_desc.text: As a small child, [CHARACTER.GetShortUINameNoTooltipNoFormat] struck Balerion the Black Dread upon the snout and laughed. A white cloak called [CharYouHerHim(CHARACTER)] brave or mad, and the court chose the kinder word.

fab_north.0001.desc.text:
Lord Brandon Stark danced at the Golden Wedding. I remember him laughing — a big grey-bearded man who called the south 'soft country' to its face and drank half the stormlords under the table to prove the point. He took ship for White Harbor with his sons and his good humour, and the North swallowed him whole.

Now a raven from Winterfell tells me the rest. Brandon Stark is dead, within the year of his homecoming, in his own bed with the snow coming down. His son Walton sits in his place — a harder man than his father, they say, quicker to draw and slower to smile.

The North has a new lord, and I have never met him.

fab_north.0002.desc.both.text:
The letter comes up from the rookery with frost still on the seal, and I read it twice before I let myself believe it.

Ser Olyver Bracken and Ser Raymund Mallery — Maegor's men, the two I spared, the two I sent to the Wall so that some good might yet be wrung out of them — have risen against their own order. Bracken has made himself a lord in all but name at Rimegate; Mallery schemes at Sable Hall. Black brothers loyal to their vows have died at the hands of black brothers who kept none.

My mercy did this. I gave them their lives, and they have spent them like counterfeit coin. The North is already stirring — the Starks do not wait on southern leave where the Wall is concerned.

fab_north.0002.desc.olyver.text:
The letter comes up from the rookery with frost still on the seal.

Ser Olyver Bracken — Maegor's man, the knight I spared and sent to the Wall — has risen against his own order and made himself master of Rimegate. Black brothers loyal to their vows have died at the hands of black brothers who kept none.

My mercy did this. I gave him his life, and he has spent it like counterfeit coin. The North is already stirring — the Starks do not wait on southern leave where the Wall is concerned.

fab_north.0002.desc.raymund.text:
The letter comes up from the rookery with frost still on the seal.

Ser Raymund Mallery — Maegor's man, the knight I spared and sent to the Wall — has raised the garrison of Sable Hall against its own officers. Black brothers loyal to their vows have died at the hands of black brothers who kept none.

My mercy did this. I gave him his life, and he has spent it like counterfeit coin. The North is already stirring — the Starks do not wait on southern leave where the Wall is concerned.

fab_north.0002.a.text: The Wall is the North's to keep. The wolves will answer.

fab_north.0002.a.tt.text: The canon course: Lord Walton Stark rides to put down the mutiny. History remembers how that ride ends.

fab_north.0002.b.text: I spared them. I will end them. Saddle Vermithor.

fab_north.0002.b.tt.text: Alt-history: the King answers his own mistake in person — and a Stark's life may hang on it.

fab_north.0003.desc.text: Word follows word up the kingsroad. Lord Walton Stark has not waited — not for my leave, not for the spring. He has called his banners in the yard where his father's bones were barely cold, taken the great blade Ice off its iron pins, and ridden north with hard men and remounts through snow a southern host would call impassable.\n\nThe free folk have a saying, the maesters tell me: the Wall is the world's edge. The Starks have a shorter one. The Wall is ours.

fab_north.0003.desc.nowalton.text: Word follows word up the kingsroad. Winterfell has not waited — not for my leave, not for the spring. The North's banners are called, and hard men with remounts push north through snow a southern host would call impassable, loyal black brothers riding at their side.\n\nThe free folk have a saying, the maesters tell me: the Wall is the world's edge. The Starks have a shorter one. The Wall is ours.

fab_north.0003.a.text: Gods go with them. Mine and theirs.

fab_north.0004.desc.text:
It is done at Rimegate, and it is done the northern way.

The mutineers held the gate two days. On the third, the loyal brothers came over the ice-slick walls with Lord Stark's men behind them, and by dusk Ser Olyver Bracken knelt in the snow of the yard he had claimed as his own. There was no trial by combat this time, no plea of old service. Lord Walton Stark heard his crimes read, took Ice in both hands, and struck the head from the man my mercy had made.

They tell me the Lord of Winterfell said only this, after: 'He died quicker than the men he betrayed.'

fab_north.0004.desc.nowalton.text: It is done at Rimegate, and it is done the northern way.\n\nThe mutineers held the gate two days. On the third, the loyal brothers came over the ice-slick walls with the North's men behind them, and by dusk Ser Olyver Bracken knelt in the snow of the yard he had claimed as his own. There was no trial by combat this time, no plea of old service. The Lord Commander heard his crimes read and struck the head from the man my mercy had made.

fab_north.0005.desc.text: Sable Hall did not fight. When word of Rimegate reached them, Ser Raymund Mallery and the last of the mutineers went over the Wall in the night — down the ice by rope and into the haunted forest, where no king's law and no lord's either has ever followed.\n\nExcept that Lord Walton Stark means to follow. His officers counselled against it; the black brothers counselled against it; the wildling guides refused outright. He is taking picked men beyond the Wall all the same. Oathbreakers who flee the king's justice, he is said to have answered, do not stop being oathbreakers for standing on the far side of it.

fab_north.0005.a.text: Come back, wolf. It is only vermin now.

fab_north.0006.desc.text:
The survivors speak of it in pieces, and the pieces do not fit together into anything a sane man wants to see whole.

They caught the mutineers' trail in the haunted forest and followed it three days into country where the trees grow older than kingdoms. On the fourth day the forest stood up. Giants — not the fireside kind, but grey-skinned and tree-tall and terrible — came out of the white silence onto the column, and the world became clubs and screaming and the smell of split pine.

They say Lord Walton Stark killed two of them. They say it took that many to bring him down. They brought back what they could carry.

fab_north.0006.a.text: Seven forgive me. I sent those men north.

fab_north.0007.desc.text:
They carried the Lord of Winterfell home to Castle Black in pieces, wrapped in his own cloak. The loyal brothers stood to honour him at the gate; the survivors of the ranging will wear the memory longer than any scar. Of Ser Raymund Mallery the wildlings later told a ranger, laughing, that the kneelers who came over the Wall had been guests at a feast — and what the feast was, I will not put to parchment.

Alaric Stark is Lord of Winterfell now. His letter acknowledging my titles is three lines long, correct in every particular, and colder than anything the Wall has ever felt.

He does not say that my mercy killed his brother. He does not need to.

fab_north.0007.a.text: The North remembers. So shall I.

fab_north.0010.desc.text:
I spared those men. Whatever they burn, whatever they break, the fire starts with me — and I will not sit in the Red Keep tallying northern dead by raven while other men pay my debts.

Vermithor rises through the cold in great bronze surges, the kingsroad a grey thread below and the snows beyond it whiter than any parchment. The Wall, when it first shows on the horizon, is a line of light like the edge of a blade.

Bracken will look up from his stolen castle and see what mercy looks like when it comes back.

fab_north.0011.desc.text:
There was no battle. There was never going to be a battle.

Vermithor came down on Rimegate's yard with a sound like the world tearing, and the mutiny ended in the time it took frightened men to open a gate. Lord Walton Stark's column, still a day's ride south, arrived to find the mutineers kneeling in rows in the snow and a dragon steaming on the ice like a mountain of banked coals.

Ser Olyver Bracken received from me at Rimegate what I should perhaps have given him beneath the Red Keep: the King's justice, delivered by the King. I did not sleep after. But no Stark died for my mercy, and no black brother either — not one, from the hour I landed.

fab_north.0011.a.text: It was mine to end. It is ended.

fab_north.0012.desc.text:
Ser Raymund Mallery went over the Wall before Vermithor's shadow ever touched Sable Hall, and there even a dragon does not follow — Vermithor would not take the ice line, and the rangers went afoot in his stead. What they brought back was a tale from the free folk, told laughing: the kneeler knight who fled the dragon had been a guest at a wildling feast, and had not left it.

Lord Walton Stark rode with me to Castle Black gate. A hard man, as they said — but at the parting he set his fist to his chest, which his household tells me he has done for no man since his father.

'You came yourself,' he said. 'The North does not forget that.'

fab_north.0012.a.text: Nor will I forget the Wall.

fab_north.0020.desc.text:
Ten years a king, and I have never seen the North. Alysanne says it plainly, over the maps: one realm cannot be half a realm the king has never stood in.

So: a great progress, to White Harbor and Winterfell and the Wall itself. And this time I mean to be clever about it. On every progress I have made, Vermithor lands and then I wait a week for my own baggage. No more. The retinue, the wardrobe, the cooks, the gifts — all of it goes AHEAD, by ship to White Harbor, and the dragons catch the column on the road.

The Queen is already choosing her ladies. She has wanted the North for years.

fab_north.0020.a.text: Proclaim it. The dragons go north.

fab_north.0020.b.text: The North has waited ten years. It can wait longer.

fab_north.0020.b.tt.text: Alt-history: cancel the progress. The Starks will hear of it — and the whole northern tale goes untold. (The Shivers still comes on schedule.)

fab_north.0021.t.text: The Envoys of Pentos and Tyrosh

fab_north.0021.desc.text:
The retinue's sails are barely over the horizon when the Free Cities arrive in my throne room.

Pentos and Tyrosh have spent three years strangling each other's trade — and half the narrow sea's with it. Now both send magisters, silk-wrapped and desperate, to beg the Iron Throne to sit between them and make a peace. It is a great honour, Barth says. It is a great snare, I say: such negotiations run long, and Winterfell is expecting me.

Alysanne cuts the knot as she always does. 'Then I shall go ahead, and you will catch me up when the ink is dry. Cancel a progress on the Starks? I would sooner insult the Wall itself.'

fab_north.0021.a.text: Go ahead of me, my love. I will not be far behind.

fab_north.0021.a.tt.text: The canon course: the Queen goes north alone, and the negotiations run far longer than anyone intends.

fab_north.0021.b.text: Pentos and Tyrosh may mend their own nets. We ride together.

fab_north.0021.b.tt.text: Alt-history: refuse the mediation. The Free Cities are slighted, but the king and queen go north side by side.

fab_north.0022.desc.text:
She goes down to the ships in the grey of morning with her ladies and her septas and half the gaiety of the court, and the docks have never been louder.

Silverwing does not take ship, of course. She circles the harbour once as the fleet stands out into the bay, silver-and-blue against the clouds, and the sailors swear the Queen's dragon means to shepherd the convoy the whole way north like a hound with her flock.

The Red Keep is very quiet by evening. I had not thought to mind it so much.

fab_north.0022.a.text: Fair winds, my Queen. I will read every raven twice.

fab_north.0023.desc.text:
Her first letter comes up from White Harbor, and I can hear her laughing through the ink.

The Manderlys have outdone themselves — a city scrubbed white as its name, mermen on every banner, a feast of lamprey and winter ale that her ladies will be recovering from for a week. And, being Alysanne, she has already done the thing no king's progress ever did: thrown open the New Castle's hall to the women of the city, high and low together, and simply listened.

The last line of her letter is less merry. 'Some of what they tell me, my love, you will need to hear. Not yet. When I am home.'

fab_north.0023.a.text: What my Queen begins, the realm ends up the better for.

fab_north.0024.desc.grudge.text:
Winterfell, her raven says, received her with every correct courtesy and no warmth at all.

Lord Alaric Stark met her in his yard, named her titles precisely, saw her retinue housed — and then gave her three days of grey silence. His brother Walton sleeps in the crypt below their feet, torn apart by giants hunting the mutineers MY mercy sent to the Wall. Alaric has never once written the accusation. He simply keeps it, the way the North keeps everything.

'He looks at me,' Alysanne writes, 'and sees your pardons. Give me time, my love. Ice melts. It only wants patience.'

fab_north.0024.desc.kingcame.text:
Winterfell, her raven says, received her with careful courtesy and a reserve that is almost, but not quite, warmth.

Lord Walton Stark is not a man who smiles at strangers — but he remembers a king who came north on dragonback to answer his own mistake, and his welcome says so in a hundred small wordless ways. It is his court that stays wary: southern queens and their silks sit oddly in a hall hung with iron swords.

'They watch me like a hawk in a henyard,' Alysanne writes, 'but the lord tells his people you came to the Wall yourself when it mattered. We begin better than I had hoped.'

fab_north.0024.desc.executed.text:
Winterfell, her raven says, received her with correct courtesy and the particular caution the North keeps for southern power.

Lord Walton Stark is a hard man to read, Alysanne writes, but there is no grief in the hall and no grudge under it — only the old northern wariness of dragons. Once, over the wine, he even offered her something like approval: his father Brandon had told him of the King's justice on Maegor's men. 'Heads, not pardons,' the old lord had said. 'The dragon judged those knights as WE would have judged them.'

'Give me a fortnight,' she writes, 'and I will have him telling me his grandfather's hunting stories.'

fab_north.0024.desc.text:
Winterfell, her raven says, received her with every correct courtesy and precious little warmth.

The Lord of Winterfell met her in his yard, named her titles precisely, saw her retinue housed — and then gave her days of grey northern silence. It is not enmity, her letter insists; it is the North's way with strangers, and a Targaryen queen with a dragon overhead is the strangest guest Winterfell has kept in living memory.

'Ice melts,' she writes. 'It only wants patience.'

fab_north.0024.a.text: If any soul alive can thaw that hall, it is she.

fab_north.0025.desc.text:
The next raven is a different bird entirely.

She has done it. Not with gifts — the North cannot be bought, she writes, and despises the attempt — but by being relentlessly, unanswerably herself. She rode out with the hunt in weather that sent half her ladies to bed. She matched the Lord of Winterfell cup for cup with honest praise for northern ale, asked after his household by name, listened to an old dispute over winter grain stores and settled it so neatly that two of his bannermen now swear by her.

And at the last, the hall watching, she set Silverwing down INSIDE the walls of Winterfell and bid the children of the castle come and touch a living dragon. 'The Lord of Winterfell laughed,' she writes, and underlines it twice. 'His own household says they had not heard it since he came to the lordship.'

fab_north.0025.a.text: The realm won her with less trouble than the North did.

fab_north.0026.desc.text:
From Winterfell she does the thing her escort dreaded and her letters had promised all along: she leaves them.

Silverwing rises out of the grey stone circle of Winterfell into a sky like polished steel, and the Queen of the Seven Kingdoms flies the kingsroad's long ghost north over the last farms, the last holdfasts, the last trees — to where the world simply stops. Her escort will be a fortnight catching her up. She means to spend that fortnight among the black brothers of Castle Black.

'The lords were scandalized,' her letter says. 'The smallfolk cheered. I find I am with the smallfolk.'

fab_north.0026.desc.together.text:
From Winterfell she does the thing her escort dreaded and I, if I am honest, had promised myself she would not: she leaves us.

Silverwing rises out of the grey stone circle of Winterfell into a sky like polished steel, and my Queen flies the kingsroad's long ghost north over the last farms, the last holdfasts, the last trees — to where the world simply stops. 'You have your lords to win,' she told me in the yard, pulling on her gloves, 'and I have my black brothers. We will trade tales when I am back.'

Her escort will be a fortnight catching her up. She does not intend to wait for them.

fab_north.0026.a.text: There has never been a queen like her. There never will be.

fab_north.0027.desc.grudge.text:
The Watch feasts her at Castle Black on salt beef, black bread and perfect honesty — and she is, she writes, entirely conquered.

But the Wall keeps its ledger too. At table an old ranger spoke, carefully, of the mutiny: of Rimegate, of the brothers who died holding to their vows, of Lord Walton Stark carried home in pieces because two of Maegor's pardoned knights thought the black too poor a coat. The Lord Commander silenced him with a look — but the silence after, she writes, had weight.

'They are too courteous to say it to their Queen. I will say it to my King. The Watch paid for the white cloaks you spared, my love. They know it. So must we.'

fab_north.0027.desc.kingcame.text:
The Watch feasts her at Castle Black on salt beef, black bread and perfect honesty — and she is, she writes, entirely conquered.

And here, at the world's edge, your name is good coin, my love. The older brothers still tell it: the winter the pardoned knights rose, and the king who did not send a raven or an army but came HIMSELF, bronze wings over Rimegate, and ended it before the North had buried a single loyal man. The Old Bear of a Lord Commander they had then is dead, but his saying survives him: 'The Iron Throne remembered us once. See that you are worth remembering twice.'

'They drink to you here,' she writes. 'I thought you should know that somewhere in your realm, men in black drink to the King.'

fab_north.0027.desc.executed.text:
The Watch feasts her at Castle Black on salt beef, black bread and perfect honesty — and she is, she writes, entirely conquered.

One thing surprised her. She had expected, delicately, some grievance over Maegor's knights — the white cloaks who might have come to the Wall and did not, because the King gave them the sword instead. She found the opposite. 'Kings mean well when they empty their dungeons on us,' the Lord Commander told her over the wine. 'They send us their traitors and call it mercy. Your king sent us no one he could not trust to us. The Watch has thanked worse men for better gifts.'

'It seems,' she writes, 'that the harder choice was the kinder one, here. I am still deciding what I think of that.'

fab_north.0027.desc.exiled.text:
The Watch feasts her at Castle Black on salt beef, black bread and perfect honesty — and she is, she writes, entirely conquered.

At table there was one hard toast. Maegor's knights, the ones the King spared and sent across the narrow sea — the Watch has heard the tales of them selling their swords in Essos, oathless and comfortable, and the black brothers find it bitter beer. 'Every lordling in chains is offered the Wall,' an old ranger said. 'It seems a white cloak buys a softer sentence.' The Lord Commander did not silence him.

'They would have taken those knights, my love,' she writes, 'and been glad of the swords. Remember the Wall, next time mercy is in your gift.'

fab_north.0027.desc.text:
The Watch feasts her at Castle Black on salt beef, black bread and perfect honesty — and she is, she writes, entirely conquered.

They showed her the ice cells and the winch cage, the armory with its thousand old swords, the ledgers with their terrible arithmetic: a Wall built for ten thousand held by hundreds. She asked the Lord Commander what the Watch needed and he laughed and said 'everything', and then, seeing her face, stopped laughing and began to answer honestly. The list ran to a second sheet.

'I came north expecting to admire a wonder,' she writes. 'I have found nine hundred poor and honest men holding up the sky, and I mean to do something about it.'

fab_north.0027.a.text: Read me the list again. All of it.

fab_north.0028.desc.text:
One letter I will keep until I die.

'Three times I put her at it, my love. Three times. I meant only to fly beyond the Wall and back — to see the haunted forest from above, to say a queen had done it. Silverwing has never refused me anything. She refused me this. Each time we came over that ice she screamed and shore away south, and no urging of mine could hold her to the line. The third time I felt it myself — I cannot write what it was. A cold that is not cold. A NO as wide as the world.

Whatever the Wall is, Jaehaerys, it is not only ice. Our dragons know something we do not. I sat in the snow at Castle Black a long while after, and the Lord Commander said nothing, and I was grateful to him for it.'

fab_north.0028.a.text: Whatever wards that Wall, gods grant it never fails.

fab_north.0028.b.text: Even dragons know where the world ends. My Queen found the edge.

fab_north.0029.desc.text:
She is back at Winterfell when the long letter comes — the one she promised at White Harbor, written in a harder hand than her usual.

At every stop of this progress she has held her women's courts: the hall cleared of lords, the doors opened to any woman who would speak, from the fishwives of White Harbor to the black brothers' washerwomen of Mole's Town. Two things fill the letter. The first is the Watch: nine hundred men holding a hundred leagues of ice on a beggar's portion, while good land south of the Wall lies under lords who never look north. She has an idea about that, she writes, and I am to be ambushed with it at Winterfell.

The second thing she will not put in writing at all. 'It concerns an old right of lords, and the women it is used upon. When you have heard what I have heard, you will end it. I know you.'

fab_north.0029.desc.together.text:
She comes back to Winterfell out of a snow squall, wind-burned and grave, and that first evening she does not tell stories at table the way she has at every other stop of this progress.

Later, by the fire in our chambers, she gives me both halves of what the North has given her. The first is the Watch: nine hundred men holding a hundred leagues of ice on a beggar's portion, while good land south of the Wall lies under lords who never look north. She has an idea about that, and she means to make it in front of Lord Stark's whole court, where it cannot be quietly declined.

The second she says very quietly, watching the fire. 'It concerns an old right of lords, and the women it is used upon. When we are home, my love, I will tell you what my women's courts have told me — and then you will end it. I know you.'

fab_north.0029.a.text: Then let me get north, and be ambushed.

fab_north.0030.desc.text:
Two months, now. Two months of Pentoshi arithmetic and Tyroshi theatre.

Every point conceded is reopened the next morning in different silks. The Tyroshi archon's men walked out twice this week over the wording of a preamble — a PREAMBLE — and the Pentoshi magisters smiled so widely at that reversal that I nearly had the whole pack of them shipped home in the same hull to finish their war at sea.

And every third day a raven from the North lands like sunlight on this table: my Queen is winning Winterfell, feasting with black brothers, flying at the edge of the world. Half a year I promised her at most. The ink is nowhere near dry.

fab_north.0030.a.text: Barth, tell the archon's men the preamble stands. All of it.

fab_north.0031.desc.text:
Done. Signed, sealed, sworn before gods old, new and whatever the Tyroshi keep in those painted temples of theirs. Pentos and Tyrosh have their peace; the narrow sea has its trade lanes back; the Iron Throne has the thanks of two Free Cities and, rather more usefully, their tariff concessions.

Half a year, near enough to make no matter. Alysanne left in one season and writes to me from another.

Winterfell is a long way north, and I am done with waiting.

fab_north.0031.a.text: North, and swiftly. Make ready to travel — I will not wait another day.

fab_north.0031.a.tt.text: Begin the journey to Winterfell. In the travel menu the King may take Vermithor and arrive within days, or ride if he wishes. (Cancelling the travel plan will not strand the story.)

fab_north.0031.b.text: By the kingsroad, with a proper column — let the North SEE its king come.

fab_north.0031.b.tt.text: Begin a slow progress up the kingsroad to Winterfell, with all the pomp of a royal column, and the road will have its own tales. (Cancelling the travel plan will not strand the story.)

fab_north.0033.desc.grudge.text:
Lord Alaric Stark receives me in the yard of Winterfell with every honour the law requires and not one gesture more.

His courtesies are exact. His eyes are his brother's tomb. Alysanne warned me — half a year of her warmth has bought me the difference between hostility and correctness, no further — and still the cold of that yard reaches through the furs. This is the lord whose brother rode north to clean up after MY mercy and came home in pieces.

At the doors he pauses. 'Before you feast, Your Grace,' he says, 'there is a thing in the crypts I would show you. It will not take long. The dead keep short courts.'

fab_north.0033.desc.kingcame.text:
Lord Walton Stark receives me in the yard of Winterfell, and for a moment the grim face and the grey furs are all I see — and then he does the thing his whole court plainly did not expect: he comes down the steps and clasps my arm like a comrade.

'The last time I saw Your Grace,' he says, 'you were a length of bronze wings over Rimegate, and the worst winter's work of my life was ended before my column ever reached it. I have told the tale often. Now they can all stop believing I invented it.'

Behind him, Alysanne is laughing. The North is cold. This hall, tonight, will not be.

fab_north.0033.desc.executed.text:
Lord Walton Stark receives me in the yard of Winterfell with the grave, unhurried courtesy of a man who kneels rarely and means it when he does.

'My father Brandon spoke of you, Your Grace,' he says as we climb the steps. 'He came home from the Golden Wedding saying the south had made itself a proper king at last — one who gave Maegor's dogs heads instead of pardons. He said the North judges a man by what he does with a sword when a debt is owed. He judged you fit.'

From a Stark, Alysanne murmurs at my shoulder, that is a wedding feast, a tourney and a triumph all together.

fab_north.0033.desc.together.text:
Winterfell receives us both in a yard swept clean as a sept floor, and the Lord of Winterfell honours us with precise, measured, wholly unreadable northern courtesy.

We came north side by side — dragons above the retinue's long column, the Free Cities' envoys sent home to mend their own nets — and if the crowds of the winter town cheered the spectacle, the hall of Winterfell reserves judgement. The North does not warm to visitors for arriving impressively.

Alysanne squeezes my arm as the doors boom shut behind us. 'Patience, my love. Ice melts. I have done this before.'

fab_north.0033.desc.text:
Lord Stark receives me in the yard of Winterfell with every honour the law requires and the particular guarded stillness the North keeps for dragons.

Alysanne's half-year of warmth has gone before me and made the way smoother than it might have been: the hall is correct, the feast is laid, the words are all the proper words. But the eyes that watch me down the length of that smoky hall belong to lords whose fathers knelt to mine under threat of fire, and none of them have forgotten it.

Winterfell will be won the way Alysanne won it, or not at all: slowly.

fab_north.0033.a.text: Then let us see what the North would show its king.

fab_north.0034.desc.text:
We go down with torches, past the stone kings in their rows — the Kings of Winter with their swords across their knees and their direwolves at their feet, ten thousand years of them staring blind into the dark. Lord Alaric says nothing the whole descent.

He stops at a tomb newer than the rest, the stone still pale. The likeness is of a big man with a blade across his knees, and I do not need the name read to me.

'My brother Walton,' Alaric says. 'He took Ice north against the men Your Grace sent to the Wall, and beheaded the first of them with it. The others he chased beyond the Wall, into the haunted forest. The giants tore him into five pieces. We buried what came back.' He raises the torch, and his eyes come to mine at last. 'You spared those knights, Your Grace. I have wondered these eight years what it is a king says to that.'

fab_north.0034.a.text: Your brother paid my share of that mercy. I am sorry, Lord Stark.

fab_north.0034.b.text: (Say nothing. The dead ask for nothing.)

fab_north.0035.desc.kingcame.text: There is no tomb to visit, and no grudge kept above one. Instead there is a feast — and at the high table, a Lord of Winterfell telling his bannermen, once more and by popular demand, the tale of the winter the King came north.\n\n'Rimegate was to be MY grave, like as not,' Walton Stark says, with the grim satisfaction the North reserves for its narrowest escapes. 'Storming a Wall castle in a mutiny winter — ask the Watch what that costs. And then the sky rattled, and the mutineers' gate opened, and the whole cursed business was done before my column cleared the Gift.' He raises his cup to me, and the hall comes up with him. 'To the debt the King paid HIMSELF, sers. The North remembers good as well as ill.'

fab_north.0035.desc.executed.text:
There is no tomb to visit and no grudge in this hall — only a feast, and a Lord of Winterfell who unbends over the course of it from granite to mere oak.

It is late, and the fires low, when Walton Stark speaks of it at last. 'My father used to say your justice bought this peace, Your Grace. Maegor's knights, the ones you gave the sword.' He turns his cup slowly. 'Men called it harsh in the south, I am told. No northman called it so. Oathbreakers sent to the Wall are oathbreakers still — the Watch has buried brothers for lesser mercies. You spent six heads to spare it that. Winterfell counts the bargain cheap.'

Alysanne catches my eye down the table. LISTEN, her look says. The North is telling you it trusts you.

fab_north.0035.desc.text:
There is no tomb to visit and no old wound under this hall — only a feast in the northern manner, which is to say: enormous, unhurried and honest.

The Lord of Winterfell drinks with me, speaks of harvests and wolf packs and the state of the kingsroad, and somewhere past midnight — the precise moment is hard to fix — I understand that I have stopped being inspected and started being hosted. Alysanne's half-year of groundwork, spent in a single evening.

The North gives nothing quickly. What it gives, it means.

fab_north.0035.a.text: To Winterfell, then. And to patient queens.

fab_north.0036.desc.text:
She ambushes me at Winterfell, exactly as promised, and she does it before the assembled court, which is how I know she means to win.

'The Night's Watch holds a hundred leagues of Wall on a beggar's portion,' my Queen says. 'Nine hundred men, where ten thousand once stood, feeding themselves off Brandon's Gift while the lords south of it grow fat facing the wrong way. I ask the King to double the Watch's lands: every league of it south of the Gift, from the one sea to the other. Let it be called the New Gift, and let the Wall eat.'

The hall has gone very quiet. The lords whose lands those are stand along it like standing stones. Lord Stark's face is shut. The Lord Commander's men, down-table, have stopped breathing.

fab_north.0036.a.text: It shall be done. The New Gift, to the Watch, in perpetuity.

fab_north.0036.a.tt.text: The canon grant: the counties of the New Gift pass to the Lord Commander of the Night's Watch. The Watch will not forget it — and the northern lords will not forget it either.

fab_north.0036.b.text: The Wall has land enough. The North keeps its own.

fab_north.0037.desc.text:
In the new-given lands there is a village on a lake, with a stone towerhouse on a holm reached by a hidden causeway, and it is there the Queen's progress shelters on its last northern night.

The village women feast her on what they have. In the morning, as the column forms up, Alysanne unpins the golden circlet from her hair — the one she has worn the length of this progress — and sets it in the hands of the village elder, to be kept by the place forever in memory of a queen's stay.

They are calling the village Queenscrown before the column is out of sight. They will be calling it that, I suspect, when everyone who could say why is ten centuries dust.

fab_north.0037.a.text: The North will keep that crown longer than any vault of mine.

fab_north.0038.desc.text:
South again — wings and sails and the long column unwinding down the kingsroad, out of the snows and into autumn country where the air stops hurting.

King's Landing smells of smoke and salt and too many people, which is to say: of home. The city gives its King and Queen a roaring welcome; the court gives us a mountain of petitions; and Alysanne, who charmed Winterfell and feasted with black brothers and set her dragon at the edge of the world, looks down at the Red Keep from Silverwing's back, she tells me, with something like disappointment that it is over.

It is not quite over. There is a thing she heard in the North that she has been waiting the whole road home to lay before me.

fab_north.0038.a.text: Then let us hear it. All of it.

fab_north.0039.desc.text:
She comes to me not as my wife but as a petitioner, and she brings her women's courts with her — every hall from White Harbor to Mole's Town, every voice that spoke when the lords were sent out of the room.

'The right of the first night,' Alysanne says. 'The lord's claim to a bride before her husband. The maesters call it old custom and the lords call it seldom used, and I have sat with the women it was used upon. In the North, in the riverlands — everywhere, my love. It is not custom. It is a cruelty with a pedigree. No law of gods or men should suffer it, and you are the law of men.'

She sets no scroll before me. She only waits. She told me at Winterfell she knew what I would do when I had heard what she had heard.

fab_north.0039.a.text: Then hear the law of men: the first night is ABOLISHED, everywhere.

fab_north.0039.a.tt.text: The canon reform: Queen Alysanne's women's courts end the right of the first night throughout the Seven Kingdoms.

fab_north.0039.a.lords_tt.text: The great northern lords who kept the old right will resent it — a small, lasting grievance against both the King and the Queen.

fab_north.0039.b.text: The lords' old rights are the lords' affair. I will not reach into their halls.

fab_north.0040.desc.text:
The magisters of Pentos and Tyrosh are sent home with fair words, no treaty and identical expressions of silk-wrapped outrage, and I find I can live with that.

The retinue is already at sea. The court is scandalized twice over — once that the Iron Throne declined the honour of mediating, and once more that the King and Queen mean to make the whole progress side by side, two dragons over one column, like some tale out of the Conquest.

Alysanne is entirely unrepentant. 'They will forgive you a lost treaty,' she says, pulling on her riding gloves. 'The North would never have forgiven us a lost progress.'

fab_north.0040.a.text: Two dragons north, then. The realm will look up.

fab_north.0040.b.text: The kingsroad, together — a true royal progress, every league of it.

fab_north.0041.desc.text:
Vermithor and Silverwing take the kingsroad's line north wingtip to wingtip, bronze and silver against the winter sky, and below us the realm comes out of doors to watch its King and Queen pass over.

The Neck crawls beneath like a drowned world; then the North opens, white and endless, and Alysanne's laughter carries across the gap between our dragons in scraps whenever the wind allows. She has wanted this for ten years: the two of us, the cold clean air, the world made small.

Grey towers on the horizon. Winterfell rising. Let us see what the North makes of two dragons come courting.

fab_north.0041.a.text: Down, now. Courtesy waits in that cold yard.

fab_north.0091.desc.text:
The column makes its leagues in the old way, and I begin to understand what I have been missing from dragonback all these years.

A king on a dragon is an omen; a king on the road is a MAN, and the smallfolk come out to see the difference. They line the hedgerows with their children on their shoulders. They bring petitions, ale, complaints about the local septon, one goat (a gift; we kept it). At every halt the tent of petitions fills, and I do more small justice in a week of mud than in a month of throne room.

The baggage train, for once, is exactly where I am.

fab_north.0092.desc.text:
The causeway through the Neck is a spear-haft of dry ground laid across a green-brown drowned world, and the column walks it two abreast with the bog breathing on either side.

The crannogmen do not show themselves, and show themselves constantly: a reed screen that was not there an hour ago, a child's woven charm hung at the road's edge, once a spear standing upright in the mud a long bowshot out — planted, the guides say, as a courtesy. Greywater Watch is somewhere out there, moving, as it always is.

The men do not love this road. I find I do. No army has ever forced it, and no dragon is needed to hold it: the Neck holds itself.

fab_walton_grudge_opinion.text: Blames the King for his brother's death

fab_new_gift_resentment_opinion.text: Gave northern lands to the Watch

fab_kings_sorrow_opinion.text: Owned the cost of his mercy

fab_first_night_lords_opinion.text: Abolished the lord's right of the first night

fab_rego.0001.desc.shivers.text:
Lord Rego Draz is dead in the mud of Flea Bottom, and I am told there was not enough left of his head to close his eyes.

He was being carried from the Red Keep to his manse on the Street of Silk, in that gilded palanquin this city has laughed at for ten years. In the heart of Flea Bottom a crowd closed around him. A dozen men, hungry, half in drink, and full of the same talk that has run through my streets since the cold came - that bread costs three times what it did, that the Shivers came ashore off a ship, and that the man who counts the king's coin is a Pentoshi. His bearers set him down and ran.

One of them worked a cobblestone loose from the street I paved and brought it down on him again and again until the work was done.

I made Rego a lord because the magisters of Pentos would not have him, low-born and rich as he was. He had no land, no castle, no sworn sword; my own court named him the Lord of Air for it, and he laughed louder at that jest than any man in the hall. He filled my treasury for eleven years and never once lied to me about a figure. He was murdered a quarter mile from my gates for having been born across the narrow sea.

#bold There is a stone somewhere in Flea Bottom with my friend's blood on it, and a hand that lifted it. #!

fab_rego.0001.desc.text:
